Raleigh’s housing reforms helped ease rents, Pew study finds

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing.
  • Recent findings suggest that following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found.
  • The report highlights how adding latest housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing. Latest research from The Pew Charitable Trusts shows what happened when Raleigh, N.C., followed that playbook.

Recent findings suggest that following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found. The result was a building boom, particularly for the townhomes and apartments the city’s earlier rules constrained. This uptick in homebuilding made renting more affordable in North Carolina’s capital city, especially for middle-income households and younger residents.

The report highlights how adding latest housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minn., and Austin, Texas. The same dynamic is playing out across the Sun Belt, where many of the nation’s fastest-growing metros also have some of the loosest zoning rules, and where rents and home prices have dropped more dramatically than anywhere else in the country.

It has been revealed that raleigh didn’t rely on a single fix to make building housing easier. Its reforms combined a rewrite of its form-based code, an end to parking minimums, denser building near transit and a housing bond to support affordable housing.

“Of all of the drivers of housing costs – population growth, an influx of high-income earners, high land costs and high construction costs – we have the most agency and direct control over restrictive zoning regulations,” Patrick Young, Raleigh’s planning and development director, said in a statement.

Raleigh’s 2021 zoning reform, which expanded the city’s already-established form-based code, opened the door to more “missing middle” housing. It did so by replacing units-per-acre caps with physical standards such as lot size, yards, and building height.

The changes legalized duplexes, triplexes and quadplexes in more residential districts and expanded where townhomes can be built. Under the new form-based code, further refined in 2022, builders can now construct small apartment buildings and tiny houses with up to two dwelling units on compact infill lots.

As a result, builders can now construct missing middle housing in more of Raleigh’s neighborhoods, a shift that Pew links to better affordability for middle-income and younger residents.

According to recent reports, raleigh eliminated its citywide parking minimums in 2022. That allowed developers to fit more housing units on each property and, in some cases, spared them the expense of building costly parking structures, which can often make a project too costly to pursue.

The city also spurred housing growth by allowing taller, denser buildings near major transit corridors. Transit Overlay District zones allowed for an extra story along Bus Rapid Transit corridors, extending half a mile along some local bus routes.

Additionally, a density bonus allows developers to exceed height limits by up to 50% if at least 20% of the extra units are designated as affordable, below-market units.

The City of Raleigh approved an $80 million housing bond in 2020 that is projected to create at least 700 affordable homes, fund homebuyer assistance and help homeowners with home repairs.

About $14 million has already gone to four developments totaling more than 240 units, while another $24 million in gap financing will back over 470 additional units, more than 90% of which will be affordable to households earning 60% of area median income or less.

Between 2021 and 2024, Raleigh added 16,884 housing units, growing its housing stock by 7.7%, even as the city’s population grew by 5.8% over the same period. Raleigh’s housing growth also outpaced the state (5.7%) and national (3.2%) rates during that period.

It has been revealed that of the 16,884 units added, roughly 2,000, or 12%, were affordable to households earning 80% or less of area median income (AMI), with Raleigh’s housing bond funds helping support their development. Density bonuses contributed about 200 of those affordable units, accounting for 10% of the total.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, Raleigh’s code changes intentionally shifted a large share of production away from detached single-family homes toward townhomes, duplexes and tiny homes. Since 2021, the city has issued more than twice as many townhouse permits as in 2015 to 2020, and has permitted more than 200 duplex units and over 200 accessory dwelling units (ADUs).

It has been revealed that as a result, average monthly rents rose at only half the national pace and fell in real, inflation-adjusted terms. Pew’s analysis estimates inflation-adjusted rents declined 15% from 2022 to 2025, and, as of 2025, the income needed to afford the city’s median rent dropped from 79% of AMI to 65%.

Raleigh’s experience mirrors a wider trend among fast-growing Sun Belt markets, where less restrictive zoning and fewer barriers to housing development have supported greater housing production and helped moderate housing costs. The South accounted for more than half of all U.S. housing starts between 2021 and 2025, while Sun Belt markets continue to lead the nation in rent and home price declines.

It has been revealed that according to Yardi Matrix’s October 2026 multifamily report, rents fell year over year in 12 major US markets. The Sun Belt accounted for ten of those, led by Austin, Houston, Nashville, Tampa and Phoenix. The for-sale market indicates a similar pattern, with home prices dropping disproportionately in the Sun Belt while climbing in the Northeast and Midwest.

Georgia builders give affordable housing an essential new identity

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Put an affordable housing project on a planning commission agenda, and the neighborhood naysayers come out of the woodwork to fight.
  • Industry observers note that they argue it will destroy the neighborhood’s character.
  • An affordable home – or neighborhood – by any other name is still affordable, no?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Put an affordable housing project on a planning commission agenda, and the neighborhood naysayers come out of the woodwork to fight.

Industry observers note that they argue it will destroy the neighborhood’s character. Labeling the development as workforce housing doesn’t help much.

What’s in a name? An affordable home – or neighborhood – by any other name is still affordable, no? Still, companies rebrand when the current brand is struggling. And Georgia homebuilders and land developers are taking a crack at giving “affordable housing” a brand makeover, one that’s less stigma and more economic and social fabric dynamism.

The Georgia Residential Land Development Council and the Home Builders Association teamed up to dub affordable housing “essential homes.” They are pairing it with a tagline: “Homes for the people who keep Georgia working.”.

But defining essential homes as housing that workers can afford near where they work could be applied broadly as lawmakers from the federal to local levels wrestle with how to make housing more affordable.

It has been revealed that “It’s a reality nationally that the buying power of the average American is not considered in land use and zoning policies,” Jay Knight, GRLDC’s chairman, told HousingWire TBD. “Essential homes for essential people intends to move the conversation from sticks and bricks allowed to the important people being prohibited.”.

Sources indicate that the definition names no home size or price point. It asks whether the people who work in a community can afford to live there. Teachers, firefighters, nurses, first responders, healthcare workers and skilled tradespeople are among the livelihoods the term “essential” captures best. They also include younger Georgians hoping to buy a first home.

In a recent development, austin Hackney, HBAG’s executive vice president, mentioned in a statement that the term puts a human face on the affordability debate. He said that when workers can’t find homes within reach of their income, the effects reach employers, schools and local businesses.

Industry observers note that the rebrand comes with a policy push. The groups say zoning restrictions, long permit reviews, infrastructure requirements and delayed final plat approvals add substantial costs that end up in home prices.

It has been revealed that GRLDC helped advance Senate Bill 447, which took effect July 1. The law sets timelines and accountability for Georgia’s land disturbance permit reviews. The council’s next target is final plat and bond reform. It wants reasonable approval timelines, standardized bonding requirements, and an end to delays that keep completed developments from moving forward.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development considers housing affordable when occupants pays no more than 30% of gross income on housing costs. Programs add other definitions, often tied to area median income. Affordable housing typically targets households at 60% of the area median income or less, while workforce housing covers roughly 60% to 120%.

According to recent reports, workforce housing, however, isn’t explicitly defined in federal law or regulation, according to a March 2026 Congressional Research Service analysis. But the term is used to avoid saying a housing development is affordable housing.

Opposition often centers on neighborhood character. Researchers also find residents may fear newcomers’ socioeconomic status more than the buildings themselves. Property values are another common worry, though research cited by the Florida Housing Coalition found almost no negative effect on neighboring market-rate homes.

Knight said the definition problem became clear at a speaking engagement. He asked a room of roughly 40 people to define affordable housing. One woman said Section 8. Someone else said anything under $400,000. A person from the Northeast thought it meant rent control.

Knight said that convinced him people weren’t talking about the same thing, which made the conversation unproductive. His business partner suggested essential homes. Knight said the organizations liked it immediately.

Terms such as affordable homes, starter homes, first-time buyer or workforce housing arrive with a definition already attached. Knight mentioned “essential homes” encourages people to ask what it means, which gives the groups a chance to set the definition themselves.

Sources indicate that the rationale behind the rebranding is that if local governments can dictate what can be built, the standard shouldn’t exceed what their own employees can buy. Knight stated the average municipal employee earns about $60,000 to $62,000 a year in Georgia. That means they can afford about a $225,000 home.

According to recent reports, in most U.S. markets today, that would buy roughly 1,100 square feet on a 35-foot detached lot, with no garage and no homeowners association, he said. He added that would put the price at about three and a half times annual income, close to the ratio GIs returning from World War II paid in the late 1940s and 1950s.

Recent findings suggest that knight said zoning conditions have pushed home prices to a much higher ratio. High-cost areas like California, Newly introduced York and Florida are prime examples. In Silicon Valley, the median home price is 11.4 times median household income, according to an annual report from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. The Miami metro’s ratio is 7.6.

Industry observers note that high prices relative to income are a major reason the median first-time homebuyer is now 40. It’s an all-time high, according to the National Association of Realtors. Such a disparity is why California and Florida have been at the forefront of housing reforms.

The Georgia campaign will put faces to the term: a police officer, a teacher, a nurse and a forklift operator. Knight remarked it will portray the kinds of workers that municipalities court with industry.

Industry observers note that knight, who sits on an advisory council for the National Association of Home Builders, stated he has shared the term with the executive director of the Houston Home Builders Association. He said Houston is now discussing it, since builders nationwide are having the same conversations.

“Who can be against essential housing?” Knight mentioned.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.
  • Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, revealed a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, revealed a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the organization plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

In a recent development, sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, stated Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a really crucial blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he noted. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky stated. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Industry observers note that batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky mentioned Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently unveiled aims for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky noted.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • In a recent development, most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

In a recent development, most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

It has been revealed that according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

In a recent development, zecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

It has been revealed that together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

Recent findings suggest that october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

It has been revealed that at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

Industry observers note that NU7 does not introduce a latest transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

Sources indicate that ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

Industry observers note that as of ZecStats' latest revision on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who blueprint to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

It has been revealed that in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. People need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

In a recent development, the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

Recent findings suggest that that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Recent findings suggest that every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

According to recent reports, the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

Shiba Inu’s layer-2 network, Shibarium, is experiencing a major slowdown as daily network activity has fallen to three-digit figures (fewer than 1,000 transactions), hitting lows not seen in months.

In a recent development, shibarium processed 546 transactions, according to Shibariumscan data, marking a slower period for the layer-2 network after activity spiked to a high of 6,370 on October 31, 2026. Transaction activity declined afterward, and the decline intensified amid the sell-off that hit the market in recent weeks.

The latest figures suggest that fewer transactions are taking place across Shibarium compared with periods of stronger activity. The key question now is whether Shibarium can regain momentum in the coming weeks.

Meanwhile, development continues behind the scenes for the Shiba Inu layer-2 network, as long-time Shiba Inu community member and developer Mazrael revealed a significant batch of contracts deployed on Puppynet, Shibarium's testnet.

But in the meantime, Shibarium’s fall to three-digit activity levels is a major slowdown that SHIB holders and ecosystem watchers will be watching closely.

Shiba Inu's on-chain holders increased as the number of wallets holding SHIB hit 1,700,930 on November 19, 2026.

According to the latest figures shared by Etherscan SHIB, an X account dedicated to providing updates on the SHIB ecosystem, the cryptocurrency added 236 newly introduced on-chain holders in a single day, taking its total past the 1.7 million milestone.

Recent findings suggest that the month of November has also seen consistent growth, with SHIB adding 4,520 holders since the start of the month. The broader 2026 trend is even more pronounced, with the number of holders of the token increasing by 152,300 since the beginning of the year.

While Shiba Inu's latest milestone seems remarkable, Mazrael suggested that the Shib ecosystem, including Shibarium, might have more holders than indicated, with 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on the BNB Chain.

Industry observers note that "Shibarium has more holders than those you listed, though. But yeah. Well, there are also 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on BNB. But that's not actually CCIP SHIB; it is a peg," Mazrael wrote.

Breaking: AI agent provider Sierra closes $1.75B investment amid rapid revenue growth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, six months after its last funding round, artificial intelligence startup Sierra Technologies Inc.
  • Greenoaks and Lightspeed led the Series F deal.
  • Sierra sells a set of cloud services that enables workers to create AI agents without writing code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:49 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

According to recent reports, six months after its last funding round, artificial intelligence startup Sierra Technologies Inc. today confirmed that it has closed a $1.75 billion late-stage investment.

Greenoaks and Lightspeed led the Series F deal. They were joined by a group of returning backers that included Alphabet Inc.’s GV fund.

Sierra sells a set of cloud services that enables workers to create AI agents without writing code. The centerpiece of the suite is Ghostwriter, which can automatically generate agents based on user-provided prompts and files. A software team, for example, could upload a set of bug reports and request an agent that can automatically group them by problem type.

Ghostwriter checks the dataset that users upload for formatting errors before putting it to use. Once an agent is ready, the tool simulates user conversations to find potential bugs. Ghostwriter places particular emphasis on edge cases, unusual requests that can trip up an agent if they’re not addressed during development.

Recent findings suggest that sierra also offers a second development tool called Horizon. It can be used to create agents that automate time-consuming tasks. A marketing team could build an agent that monitors user interactions with a product page over several months, finds areas for improvement and automatically makes the necessary optimizations.

Industry observers note that sierra powers customers’ agents using more than a dozen large language models. Simple requests are sent to latency-optimized LLMs, while more complex queries are processed by pricier frontier models. Sierra states that it also uses several internally developed algorithms.

Customers can manage their AI projects using a third Sierra product called Agent Studio. According to the tech giant, it includes over 40 connectors that enable agents to retrieve information from external systems. There’s also a tool for building custom connectors.

Agent Studio detects gaps in agents’ knowledge. Furthermore, it can automatically fix some of those gaps. The platform detects when a human support representative answers a customer inquiry that the help desk hasn’t encountered before and turns it into a knowledge base article. From there, agents can use the article to answer similar requests.

The studio also lends itself to certain other tasks. A collaboration feature enables multiple team members to review agent updates before they roll out to production. If a technical problem makes it past the review, developers can use a debugging tool to study what went wrong. The tool displays every single step of the workflow through which an agent processes prompts.

Rounding out Sierra’s product portfolio is an AI assistant called Explorer. It can proactively flag notable business events without a prompt and search through a tech giant’s internal datasets. In some cases, it also generates business advice.

Sierra’s latest raise, its third in 14 months, comes a few weeks after its annualized revenue topped $400 million. The manufacturer disclosed at the time that it had added nearly half the sum over the preceding quarter. Its customer base now includes half the Fortune 50.

Sierra will reportedly use the new funding to enhance its product portfolio and hire more salespeople.

#167741. The first price is the one nobody scores

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (766 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

The first price is the one nobody scores

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that agents are more confident in the comparative market analysis than they have been in years.
  • It has been revealed that that is a fair reading of what a CMA does at the kitchen table.
  • The pressure on that single day is rising.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that agents are more confident in the comparative market analysis than they have been in years. In the 2026 Survey of Best Practices for CMAs and Listing Presentations, from Giant Steps Advisors in partnership with Lone Wolf Technologies, 89.6% of 2,165 real estate professionals said they expect CMAs to become more relevant, up from 67% in 2020. HousingWire reported on October 22 that the same respondents are ready to bring AI into the work, with 83.2% very or somewhat likely to use AI-assisted CMA tools, and suggested that the lasting value of the document may lie in explaining a price rather than producing one.

It has been revealed that that is a fair reading of what a CMA does at the kitchen table. It is also an incomplete one, because it judges the document on a single day. The CMA is scored on whether it persuades the seller to sign. Whether the price it argued for held up once buyers began making offers is a question the industry has no standard way to answer.

The pressure on that single day is rising. Roughly two-thirds of agents in the survey named pricing as the leading seller objection, up from 52.7% in 2020, and 33.6% said they had lost a listing because they and the seller could not agree on a price.

It has been revealed that at the same time, the survey found that 90.8% of respondents trust the MLS above any other source for comparable sales. Similar sources, increasingly similar tools and familiar formatting tend toward similar documents. When two agents arrive with reports that look alike, the seller is left choosing between two persuasions with nothing to say which one was right last time.

It has been revealed that the industry does keep a score, but it is the wrong one for this purpose. In the National Association of Realtors 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers, the final sale price was a median of 99% of the final listing price. The final listing price is the one left standing after any reductions. A home listed too high, cut twice and then sold sits in that figure looking almost exact, because the comparison begins after the correction has already been made. Reductions are not unusual.

Redfin reported that 21.2% of listings carried a price cut in the four weeks to November 1, 2026. The figure that tells a seller how well a CMA priced their home is the sale price compared with the first asking price, but that is not the figure the industry reports.

Recent findings suggest that even the first asking price is not always the number the CMA stood behind. HousingWire’s October report noted research showing that about half of agents put a listing price in their CMA and about half do not. Where the price is left off the page, the CMA can never be checked against the outcome, because it never committed to a number in the first place.

Industry observers note that the gap widens when agents move. HousingWire reported in March that roughly 230,000 agents moved to a new brokerage in 2025, according to Courted’s 2025 State of Brokerage Recruiting and Retention Report. The sale prices stay in the closed files after an agent leaves. The judgment that set the first prices, and the sense of where that judgment ran high or low, leaves with the agent.

None of this is an argument against AI in the CMA, or against the CMA as a persuasion tool. Persuasion is part of the job, and a seller deserves an agent who can explain a price clearly and defend it under pressure. The difficulty is that the explanation is examined closely on the day it is given, while the outcome arrives months later and is measured against a different number.

It has been revealed that the industry has spent years making the valuation faster to produce and easier to present, and the survey suggests the next generation of tools will make it faster still. The question it has not yet asked is the one a seller would ask if they knew to: When this agent’s first prices met real buyers, how close did they come? Until someone asks it, every CMA will be judged on the day it persuades and never on the day the house sells.

Nikola Gojkovic is the founder of CMAflow and writes on residential valuation methodology.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

Industry News: ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too major to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too major to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” mentioned Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how massive we’re willing to dream.”.

In a recent development, the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy stated there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he mentioned. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

In a recent development, pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:.

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Industry observers note that duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy stated.

It has been revealed that AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy remarked. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy mentioned many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The upcoming products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

It has been revealed that plenty of tech giant: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he mentioned.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

In a recent development, bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Recent findings suggest that neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy stated.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Industry observers note that pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

Recent findings suggest that the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy noted. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the firm, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

Sources indicate that about 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy mentioned Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the tech giant, Duffy noted Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy mentioned Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

NEAR Protocol (NEAR) fell 11.41% on Nov. 20 and traded at $2.84, according to TradingView data. In early October, the token was trading near $6, and it has lost about half of its value since then.

Sources indicate that over the same period, the volume of NEAR Intents went up. "NEAR went from $6 to $3 in about a month. funny thing is, NEAR Intents is doing more volume now than it did in october," NEAR ecosystem contributor Evgeny Haenko wrote on X on Nov. 20.

According to Haenko, NEAR Intents averaged around $129 million in daily volume in October, and in November it was processing around $134 million a day. "The price got cut in half, the business didn't slow down at all. hard for me to be bearish here," he wrote.

NEAR Intents lets people swap assets across more than 30 blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP. The service is built into wallets such as Ledger, Trust Wallet and Brave. Over the past year, its trading volume grew 7.1 times to $39.5 billion.

Recent findings suggest that NEAR Intents has collected about $63 million in fees in total, and the network keeps about 29% of that amount. Fees on the NEAR Intents interface, payments from B2B partners and the spread on better-than-market trades accounted for 16.3%, 9.9% and 2.8% of the fees, respectively. Over the last 30 days, the protocol earned about $1.8 million, compared with $2.2 million in October.

Since February 2026, the protocol has used NEAR Intents revenue to buy NEAR on the market. More than 1.84 million NEAR have gone to the buyback wallet so far, and that is 41.6% of all distributed onchain revenue. Base transaction fees on the network are burned in full.

According to recent reports, in early November, the NEAR community also voted to cut the maximum annual issuance from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years. The proposal, HSP-029, went through House of Stake, NEAR's governance initiative, and Haenko is one of its participants.

On Sept. 29, Bitwise released the first U.S. spot NEAR ETF on NYSE Arca under the ticker NRR. Two days later, on Oct. 1, NEAR Intents paused its services after an exploit that cost about $3.8 million, and the team promised to compensate customers in full. The exploiter later returned the funds. "The funds from the $3.8M NEAR Intents hack were sent back in full," NEAR Intents general manager Alex Shevchenko stated at the time.

UPCOMING YORK, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Caring Across Generations is contributing its expertise to Because We Care with Richard Lui in recognition of National Family Caregivers Month. Hosted by MS NOW anchor, journalist, filmmaker, author, and caregiving advocate Richard Lui, the series connects personal stories to the broader economic, workforce, and policy challenges shaping the U.S. care systems.

Launched September 9, 2026, as part of MS NOW Membership's original contributor programming, Because We Care with Richard Lui marks MS NOW as the first legacy network to launch a dedicated caregiving channel and community, convening public figures, family caregivers, and national experts to explore the realities of caregiving in America.

Caring Across Generations anchors the initiative by expanding support systems, shifting cultural norms, and advocating for policies that allow everyone to live, work, and age with dignity.

"Caregiving is the invisible foundation of  our economy, workforce, and social structures, as it is the work that makes all other work possible," noted Ai-jen Poo, Executive Director of Caring Across Generations. "Because We Care with Richard Lui amplifies caregiver experiences, reveals the complexities of our care economy, and drives momentum toward equitable policies and cultural change for care.".

Lui draws on over a decade of personal experience caring for both of his parents to fuel his advocacy, journalism, filmmaking, and technology initiatives.

Recent findings suggest that "Caring for my parents revealed how unseen this journey can be," Lui said. "Through Because We Care, we highlight critical personal stories to ensure media spotlighting translates into sustained action.".

The series highlights in-depth interviews with prominent figures from Caring Across Generations' Creative Care Council including Emma Heming Willis (caring for Bruce Willis following his frontotemporal dementia diagnosis), Yvette Nicole Brown (caring for her father with Alzheimer's while maintaining an acting career), Lauren Miller Rogen (caring for her mother, Adele, who developed early-onset Alzheimer's), Seth Rogen (supporting Lauren and her family through Alzheimer's), Sen. Andy Kim (caring for his father while raising two young children and serving in the U.S. Senate), Lisa Ling, (who spent over a decade caring for her late father through dementia before he passed away), and others. These conversations explore dementia, career balancing, family dynamics, and public policy.

In its first 60 days, Because We Care with Richard Lui assembled a roster of public figures and national caregiving experts across five interview groupings, generating at least 12 documented editorial and public audio/video placements, including coverage in eight national editorial outlets, alongside syndicated reporting and public excerpts.

This ongoing partnership reinforces a shared goal: connecting audiences with trusted caregiving resources and expanding media coverage of the care economy.

Throughout National Family Caregivers Month, Because We Care with Richard Lui continues to push caregiving to the forefront of national discourse.

ABOUT CARING ACROSS GENERATIONS.

Caring Across Generations is a national organization of family caregivers, professional care workers, disabled people and aging adults working to transform the way care is given and received in the United States. Through cultural storytelling, advocacy, coalition building and policy change, the organization works to make care accessible, affordable and equitable so everyone can live, work and age with dignity. Its work focuses on affordable childcare, aging and disability care, care work, and paid leave. Learn more at caringacross.org. Follow on social: Facebook, X, Instagram, YouTube.

It has been revealed that richard Lui is a four-time family caregiver and a Peabody- and Murrow-winning national news anchor for two decades across MS NOW, NBC News Group, CNN Worldwide, and CNA. His business career spans management consulting, corporate banking, fintech, data and artificial intelligence, including work at Oliver Wyman and Citibank, and founder of technology companies. Lui's filmmaker work includes the Academy AwardÂ®- and Grammy-qualifying caregiving documentaries Sky Blossom: Diaries of the Next Greatest Generation and UNCONDITIONAL. The author of the award-winning, bestselling HarperCollins book, Enough About Me, Lui also serves as a caregiving ambassador with AARP, Alzheimer's Association, Hilarity for Charity, and Caring Across Generations. Learn more at richardlui.com. Follow on social: Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok.

#167737. Breaking: Reducing risk by protecting trust across the real estate transaction

Breaking: Reducing risk by protecting trust across the real estate transaction

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A secure lender platform cannot protect a buyer who acts on fraudulent instructions received through another participant’s email.
  • An analysis of 668 reported wire fraud events spanning a decade identified approximately $123.8 million in reported financial exposure and approximately $11.5 million in documented losses.
  • We examine what those reported events suggest about trust, why participants outside the funding process matter and how organizations can strengthen verification across business relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A secure lender platform cannot protect a buyer who acts on fraudulent instructions received through another participant’s email. An agent’s familiar name can make a message persuasive even when the agent has no authority to move funds. For mortgage, title and real estate professionals, those connections deserve a place in the fraud prevention conversation.

An analysis of 668 reported wire fraud events spanning a decade identified approximately $123.8 million in reported financial exposure and approximately $11.5 million in documented losses. The findings point to a practical concern for everyone involved in a transaction: protecting an organization’s systems addresses only part of the risk.

We examine what those reported events suggest about trust, why participants outside the funding process matter and how organizations can strengthen verification across business relationships.

Approximately 79% of reported events, 78% of reported exposure and 80% of documented losses were associated with participants operating outside the title tech giant’s direct control. Of the 668 events reviewed, 57 resulted in documented financial loss.

According to recent reports, these figures describe the reported events analyzed. They should not be treated as an industry-wide loss rate or as proof that risk has shifted over time. Association with an external participant also does not, by itself, establish where an account was compromised or who was responsible for a loss.

Recent findings suggest that the concentration nevertheless raises an important business question. If a fraudulent request gains credibility through a customer, agent, attorney or other participant, will the next organization in the transaction recognize and verify it before someone acts?

Recent findings suggest that the traditional approach to fraud prevention focuses on authority. Organizations identify who can move money, approve payments, authorize disbursements or initiate wire transfers and then build controls around those functions.

Recent findings suggest that that remains necessary. But an attacker may also seek access to someone who influences the person sending money. Transaction details, familiar correspondence and knowledge of an approaching closing can help a fraudulent message appear credible without access to the lender’s or settlement provider’s systems.

Residential real estate transactions are particularly susceptible to this type of manipulation because they depend on trust at every stage of the process. Buyers trust agents. Sellers trust agents. Consumers trust lenders. All parties trust the professionals coordinating the transaction. Most participants are communicating with several unfamiliar parties while simultaneously navigating a process that is complex, time-sensitive and financially significant.

Recent findings suggest that for a consumer, a request that appears to come from a familiar professional may feel like part of that process. Fraud prevention must help customers distinguish a trusted relationship from a verified instruction.

Mortgage lenders, title companies, brokerages and independent professionals operate with different resources and security practices. A participant may use an email account without the monitoring or administrative oversight available within a larger organization. That difference creates a coordination challenge, not a reason to assign blame.

An agent may understand the buyer’s timeline and concerns better than anyone else. A loan officer may be the person the buyer calls when a request seems confusing. A settlement professional may be the first to see that expected funds have not arrived. Each has an opportunity to reinforce safe behavior at a different point.

According to recent reports, the strongest internal controls lose some of their value when customers receive inconsistent guidance about who will provide instructions, how to verify them or where to report a suspicious message. Those expectations should be established before the closing deadline makes every request feel urgent.

Recent findings suggest that lenders, agents and settlement providers should explain their respective roles early. Identify who will provide wiring instructions and how the customer should independently confirm them. Reinforce that guidance as closing approaches rather than relying on a single warning in an email signature.

Industry observers note that before acting on wire instructions, confirm them directly with the appropriate party using a previously established, independently verified phone number. Do not rely on a phone number supplied in the message you are trying to verify.

Sources indicate that replying to the same email thread is not sufficient because an attacker may control the account. Question unexpected changes and escalate unusual requests through your organization’s established procedures before money moves.

It has been revealed that awareness efforts should reach loan officers, agents, transaction coordinators and customer-facing staff, as well as employees authorized to disburse funds. Training should explain how a routine message or introduction can influence a consumer’s decision to trust instructions.

Sources indicate that strong email security, multifactor authentication, employee training, monitoring and incident response capabilities remain essential. Broader coordination adds to those protections. It does not reduce the need to secure accounts and systems within each business.

Organizations should identify whom to contact when instructions appear suspicious or expected funds do not arrive. Staff should know how to pause their part of the transaction, involve the appropriate settlement and lending contacts and activate established fraud response procedures. Customers need a clear way to raise concerns without feeling that they are creating an inconvenience.

In a recent development, the difference between reported exposure and documented loss in the analysis is substantial. It is consistent with the value of verification and intervention, but the totals alone do not establish which controls prevented losses or explain every event’s outcome.

It has been revealed that organizations can learn more by reviewing their own near misses. Where did a questionable request enter the process? Who recognized it? Was the customer able to reach the right person? Did a partner’s instructions conflict with the organization’s guidance? Those questions turn an avoided loss into an opportunity to improve the next transaction.

Industry observers note that wire fraud prevention is a shared responsibility across mortgage lending, title and settlement services and real estate. A participant does not need authority over funds to influence where those funds go.

The practical response is to make verification part of the customer experience from the beginning. Clear roles, consistent guidance and accessible escalation help people act safely when a familiar name or urgent request makes fraud difficult to recognize.

Successful fraud prevention frequently occurs because someone slows down, asks an additional question and verifies information before money moves.

  • Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still claims Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

In a recent development, most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It states: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

Sources indicate that the schedule is fixed. Circle revealed in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide states "message limits will tighten over time until no upcoming burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

It has been revealed that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the firm wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

In a recent development, funds already in transit are protected. The guide states "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

According to recent reports, the migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

Industry observers note that the main text above it indicates something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

In a recent development, as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle stated "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small glitch, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or enhancement integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

In a recent development, the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SUGAR LAND, Texas, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AOI (NASDAQ: AAOI), a leading provider of advanced optical and HFC networking products that power AI, today announced it has signed a multiyear long-term agreement (LTA) with an existing Tier-1 hyperscale datacenter customer.

In a recent development, under the agreement, AOI will supply the customer with 800G transceiver products as well as laser diodes over the four-year time period from December 2026 through December 2030. Other products may be added depending on future needs. The customer has agreed to purchase a minimum commitment of approximately $1.5 billion of 800G transceivers in 2027 and approximately $0.7 billion in laser diodes between 2028 and 2029. As part of the agreement, AOI will contribute a $2 million one-time expense to accelerate qualification efforts with this customer. The customer made no commitment of capital as part of this LTA.

"Securing another LTA with a second hyperscale customer provides us with meaningful long-term revenue and demand visibility, and reinforces our technology leadership, differentiated capabilities in advanced optics, and vital role in the AI infrastructure ecosystem," noted Dr. Thompson Lin, AOI's Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer. "We believe we are well positioned with our automated manufacturing capabilities and in-house laser technology to support the next phase of AI datacenter deployment.".

Recent findings suggest that lin continued, "We have a long history of manufacturing lasers and have strategically curated our portfolio to provide the high-performance optical sources driving the industry's shift toward silicon photonics, near-packaged optics (NPO), and co-packaged optics (CPO). As part of this agreement, we will be supplying our laser diodes, some of which we expect will be used to power CPO architectures, starting in 2028. We believe that in the future, CPO and related technologies will continue to drive increased demand for high-power lasers and we plan to further expand our laser manufacturing capacity in Texas to support this anticipated growth.".

It has been revealed that "The customer's forecast indicates significant demand beyond the purchase commitments specified in the agreement over its four-year term," said Dr. Stefan Murry, AOI's Chief Financial Officer and Chief Strategy Officer. "While not guaranteed, the current level of demand based on long-term discussions with the customer exceeds $10 billion over the four years of the LTA. Expanding our production capacity would position us to serve that demand, but additional sales beyond the $2.2 billion of purchase commitments specified in the agreement will depend on our ability to bring that capacity online and secure additional purchase commitments. Under the LTA, we have committed to supplying volumes needed, including a commitment to ship an agreed-upon quantity of products made in the USA, starting in the first quarter of 2027 and ramping throughout 2027. We believe this agreement supports our ability to further increase our capacity, allocate capital, and invest in advanced technologies with greater confidence. To support this accelerating customer demand, we are continuing to expand our capacity and remain focused on executing on our expansion intends.".

Estimates of future demand under the LTA are not purchase orders, binding commitments to purchase quantities beyond those already committed under the LTA, or revenue guidance. Customer discussions and forecasts may change and may not result in additional purchase commitments or orders.

Tech Report: Anthropic’s Claude Ship automates the final stage of the software development pipeline

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic PBC isn’t satisfied with having Claude just write new software.
  • Industry observers note that the company declared the launch of Claude Ship, which is a upcoming suite of artificial intelligence agents capable of automating code reviews, bug fixes and approvals.
  • Sources indicate that claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the latest bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Anthropic PBC isn’t satisfied with having Claude just write new software. With a new update today, Claude now can tell developers when the code it has generated is ready to ship into production environments.

Industry observers note that the company declared the launch of Claude Ship, which is a upcoming suite of artificial intelligence agents capable of automating code reviews, bug fixes and approvals. The last one is the most interesting of those capabilities, because code reviews and fixes are nothing new for AI. But Claude’s ability to automatically approve code changes based on the policies predetermined by an organization’s developer team is a novel development that has not been seen before.

Sources indicate that claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the latest bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools. At those organizations, fresh code is being whipped up in double-quick time, and there are also AI agents for checking that code and providing fixes if it’s not working as hoped. But until now, the final review and approval process has always been performed by humans. Claude Ship changes that.

The idea is that human developers can delegate final approval authority to Claude, so now all they really have to do is determine the quality and security standards of the code they’re asking AI to create.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line,” Anthropic remarked in a blog post. “But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code and we wanted everything after the pull request to move that fast too.”.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic stated Claude Ship consists of three parts. The first is Code Review, which is a tool that has been generally available for some time already. The other two are PR Steward and Claude Approvals, and they’re both still in beta.

PR Steward is designed to handle issues such as failing continuous integration checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review. After each push, it will leave comments on what changes were made and how to roll them back if necessary.

Once PR Steward is done, Claude Approvals takes over. It works by applying an approval policy that’s left as a file in the codebase’s repository. The approval process can incorporate various elements, including the findings in Code Review and the organization’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Sources indicate that anthropic is urging early adopters to be cautious. Because Claude Ship is still in beta, it recommends running Claude Approvals in observe-only mode first. It also advises teams to begin with just one repository first, and set monthly spending limits so they can maintain more control over everything.

Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.
  • Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.
  • The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA mentioned.

In a recent development, in its latest enhancement on the investigation, ULA mentioned it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

Industry observers note that on Tuesday, ULA stated early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp noted Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the organization looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Newly introduced Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn introduces reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA mentioned it will share more as the investigation continues.

Homebuilder underwriting works better when you name the bet

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [In the fifth of seven excerpts from his fresh book, ‘Less Wrong, More Right,’ Scott Cox argues that underwriting should identify one key assumption, then test supply, pricing power and buyer willingness with evidence.].
  • In underwriting, the money question is narrower and harder than it looks: what, specifically, is this deal depending on?
  • I once spent several weeks going back and forth with a builder about a deal he was presenting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[In the fifth of seven excerpts from his fresh book, ‘Less Wrong, More Right,’ Scott Cox argues that underwriting should identify one key assumption, then test supply, pricing power and buyer willingness with evidence.].

In underwriting, the money question is narrower and harder than it looks: what, specifically, is this deal depending on? Almost everything else in underwriting is a way of finding that one thing and then testing it.

I once spent several weeks going back and forth with a builder about a deal he was presenting. He was being sloppy about his comp analysis – overstating his market position, understating the competitive set. I knew it, and I kept pushing on it. He kept defending it. We went in circles.

It has been revealed that after a few weeks of this, he finally lost patience. “Come on, Scott,” he said. “Even if you’re right about the comps, four years from now there will be half the projects in this submarket that there are today.”.

I stopped. That’s an entirely different argument, I told him. And a completely different bet. Why didn’t you say so? Where’s the pipeline analysis? Let’s look at it.

According to recent reports, he was right, as it turned out. The supply argument was sound. And I had spent weeks pressing him on a number that – even if I’d won the argument – wasn’t the one that mattered. He hadn’t named his real bet. I hadn’t asked what it was. We were both analyzing the wrong thing.

That failure – his and mine – is the most common and most expensive mistake in underwriting. Not a specific bad assumption about costs, or an aggressive absorption rate, or a pricing premium that didn’t materialize. Those are the visible problems. The underlying one is simpler: not knowing what the deal is actually depending on, or not communicating it.

According to recent reports, every project depends on one thing being true – sometimes two, rarely three – that, if wrong, makes the deal fail to perform regardless of how well everything else turns out. It’s a premium spot with no comps – how hard can the price be pushed? It’s a rough neighborhood – with great access and it looks to be transitioning – do people take the same risk to buy as to rent here? Before there is a there there, how fast can we sell in our newly introduced MPC? Will the bond market keep buying bonds early in the life of our deal? How much competition will we have five years from now? One of these is carrying most of the weight.

Good underwriting means identifying that assumption first, then allocating effort accordingly. If the real bet is that this corridor will have half the supply in five years due to land-use and infrastructure constraints, you should be spending far more time on a detailed pipeline analysis – project by project, timing by timing – than on the precision of your current comp spread. The comp analysis matters, but it’s not the question. The question is whether the supply thesis holds.

If the real bet is that buyers will pay a premium for your product, the work is different. Have you comped the house in exhaustive detail – not category-level, but feature by feature? What do buyer-preference surveys actually show about the specific features you’re banking on? Is there evidence from comparable markets that buyers pay more for those features, in that amount? Do you know how to sell it effectively? Generic confidence in your product is not the same thing as a tested value proposition. If you can’t answer those questions specifically, you’re not underwriting the real bet – you’re hoping it works out.

Industry observers note that the problem is that most pro formas don’t reveal what they’re depending on. Effort gets distributed roughly evenly across the model – costs, absorption, pricing, schedule – with each assumption tweaked modestly in the optimistic direction. The result looks rigorous because it covers everything. But covering everything is not the same as testing the thing that matters. When several mildly aggressive assumptions sit next to each other in a spreadsheet, no one can see that one of them is critical and uncertain and the rest are secondary – which is not to say unimportant.

When I walk builders through this kind of underwriting, I sometimes hear “if we did all that and were hyper realistic as you suggest, we’d never buy anything.” I could not disagree more, and this attitude contains within it two related mistakes.

According to recent reports, one, why would having very realistic underwriting cost you deals? The only thing costing you deals is a return threshold higher than the market will allow. Is it better to have aggressive underwriting and unrealistic hurdles? Is self-deception really necessary? Two, and this is key, aggressive underwriting and unrealistic hurdles can cause you to make poor choices on deals, and deal risk.

Industry observers note that as an example, if you consistently underestimate your development schedules and costs, you have a bias against finished-lot deals – because you incorrectly think you get a sufficient premium for self-development. Realism is the path to better choices about what to do, not a hindrance to doing anything.

Adapted from Less Wrong, More Right (Part IV: Underwriting), available on Amazon.

"While AI infrastructure investments are driving tremendous growth across our data center and ATE businesses, more than two-thirds of our growth in fiscal 2026 came from non-AI-centric market opportunities. We are directing investment to three priorities: R&D that extends our technology leadership, capacity that secures supply for our customers' growth, and consistent capital returns to our shareholders," said Richard Puccio, CFO. "Our financial strength gives us the flexibility to pursue all three as we position ADI to capture the significant opportunity ahead.".
