The Best Publicity Isn’t a Headline. Here’s What Built My Business Instead.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • For 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas.
  • Almost all of my business has always come from referrals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas. I’ve put founders on morning highlights and turned product rolls out like IQBAR and Molecule Sleep into headlines. The work I love most, though, happens before any marketing campaign or pitch goes out: sitting with a founder and figuring out what they actually stand for. I know how reputations get built.

Almost all of my business has always come from referrals. In 2020, I started treating myself more like a client and following the advice I always give: build relationships before you need them, with people who’ll gladly vouch for you. I gave more talks, presented on webinars, spoke on conference panels and rolled out my newsletter. My favorite was a webinar I gave for MBA and EMBA students through BlueSteps called “LinkedIn Tips for Personal Branding.”.

It’s paid off, and it started with being more selective and intentional.

If you’re connected to me on LinkedIn, we’ve talked. That’s on purpose. I get a lot of requests, but I don’t connect just to connect.

My filter is simple: a thoughtful note, or a profile that makes me curious. When someone clears that bar, I message them, introduce myself and suggest a 15-minute intro call by phone or Zoom. You can call me while you’re commuting, cooking dinner or taking a walk. I like to get to know the person first, then the business.

LinkedIn Premium is what makes this work for me. Seeing who’s viewed my profile tells me who’s already curious, and messaging lets me reach people with a personal note instead of a cold request. It’s what I’ve always done at conferences and events: walk across the room, say hello and ask how someone’s really doing.

A couple of years ago, I reached out to someone this way. We had two phone calls. No pitch, no deck, just getting to know each other.

Recent findings suggest that after that second call, he referred me to two prospective clients. When I spoke with them, they told me something I’ll never forget: “If Michael trusts you, then we trust you.”.

It has been revealed that that sentence is the whole lesson. In PR, we talk about earned media versus paid media. Relationships work the same way. Trust that someone else earned with you and passed along is the most powerful credential you’ll ever have, and no ad can buy it.

A network you actually know pays off in another way: it’s the best search engine I have. When I need a partner or a service, I go to my network first. “Does anyone have a stellar digital growth performance agency?” gets me answers from people whose judgment I already trust, which beats a page of search results every time.

Being picky pays off here, too. Over the years, the people I know well have become my own personal advisory board.

In a recent development, the other half of building my own presence has been content. I publish a newsletter on LinkedIn called Spreading Sunshine. It’s personal by design. I share the latest in health and wellness, including my own protocols, along with business tips and a little joy. Readers tell me it feels like a note from a friend, which is exactly the point.

Industry observers note that people now reach out because of what I post. The content does the introducing for me. By the time we get on that 15-minute call, they already know what I care about, and the conversation starts three steps ahead.

In a recent development, A personal profile and a organization page do different jobs, and founders need both. SMACK! Media has its own page. When I released Anything Brands, an all-natural skin remedy balm inspired by my own family, we set up a page for it, too.

My team uses the manufacturer pages for press hits, milestones and education. My personal page is where relationships happen; the company page is where credibility lives. When a retailer, a partner or a reporter looks us up, they find a consistent story in both places, and a founder they can actually reach.

It has been revealed that treat your network like your most important client. Be selective. Be generous. Show up as a human.

Ready to put that into practice? LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make those 15-minute conversations easier to start.

My favorite part is still the people: hearing about a founder’s significant win, how someone got through a tough quarter, their kids, their dogs, how they juggle it all. If one of those calls leaves someone a little less burned out, that’s part of what fuels my positivity and boundless energy.

In a recent development, some of my best relationships started with someone on the other end of the line, a little out of breath from a walk or with dinner sizzling in the background. Those calls rarely feel like business. After 30 years, I’ve learned the best publicity isn’t a headline. It’s someone who knows you saying your name in a room you’re not in. That’s exactly what Michael did for me. Treating myself like a client has been the best campaign I’ve ever run.

  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a major decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

According to recent reports, nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Substantial Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a major decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

Sources indicate that the offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

According to recent reports, all of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in newly introduced hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the organization decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a tech giant right now?

It has been revealed that harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

It has been revealed that but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one manufacturer.

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

According to recent reports, the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

Industry observers note that AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Sources indicate that hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual manufacturer. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a manufacturer.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the significant platforms will copy anything that works.

It has been revealed that the true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

Industry observers note that the bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

It has been revealed that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

In a recent development, 2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a manufacturer that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

According to recent reports, there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

According to recent reports, other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a manufacturer of their own or a year with their family.

Your Customers Just Got an AI Agent. Is Your Business Ready to Talk to Them?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies.
  • Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very crucial questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

From the consumer’s perspective, a personal agent fights the battles they don’t want to, and does so more rigorously than they ever could.

In a recent development, someone’s flight gets cancelled, and their personal agent can argue with the airline until it gets a credit. Someone points it at subscription services and gets every one to offer a discounted rate. I’ve seen dozens of these examples pile up on social media over the past few weeks, and the pattern is always the same. A task a person would normally decide was not worth the trouble is now getting done anyway, because an agent has no concept of trouble.

We used to think about bots talking to bots like something that will happen “someday.” It’s happening now. For consumers who don’t want to solve problems through sheer persistence and patience, this is an exciting development. For businesses that have built their customer service programs around interacting with humans, this is a challenge to solve, fast.

Sources indicate that the simple response to this innovation sounds like: “We need our policies to be accurate, because AI will be better at calling us out on them than a human customer.” It goes deeper than that. Every refund policy and guarantee clause has fine print and phrases that are ever so slightly open to interpretation. Personal AI agents can read these policies and find where they bend in ways a human never could.

And they’ll do this at scale. One customer raising a question and finding a loophole is a cost of doing business. Thousands of agents doing the same thing can overwhelm a business, both financially and operationally.

Recent findings suggest that that kind of volume does not behave like a normal surge in customer support demand. It behaves more like a denial-of-service attack. Nobody debates whether each individual request is legitimate; the volume itself is the problem. The response has to be infrastructural: detecting, filtering, a real system for deciding what gets through. “We will deal with it when it happens” is not a strategy at this scale.

Retail and travel may seem like the industries most vulnerable to risk, but any business with documented policies faces the same exposure. Insurance, financial services, healthcare — wherever a organization has put a promise or statement of intent in writing, an agent can find it and act on it.

AI has already carved out a massive role in how businesses interact with customers. Now it’s showing up on the other side of the conversation. Nobody has every single answer for how to prepare for this new reality, us included. But there are foundational moves worth making now, rather than waiting for the rest of the industry to decide what to do.

According to recent reports, first, there’s the question of identity. Most businesses have no reliable way to know whether they are talking to a customer, a customer’s authorized agent or something pretending to be one. That infrastructure needs to be in place before anything else matters.

Second, you need visibility into what is already happening. You need to be able to see how often an agent is showing up in a support queue, what it’s asking for and how often it’s succeeding.

Then there’s the problem of the policies themselves. A traditional review to ensure accuracy is no longer sufficient. Businesses need to audit their policies, line by line, and stress-test every potential ambiguity that could turn into a vulnerability. Find the gaps before an agent does.

Resist the instinct to default to blocking. Throughout history, we’ve seen what happens to companies that try to close a door that’s going to be kicked down regardless. Search engines that tried to wall off the open web lost to the ones that stayed open, and the same pattern is likely to repeat here. Open does not mean undefended. It means building real verification and governance instead of a blanket “no,” even while the rest of the playbook is still being written.

In a recent development, major players are picking sides right now, with Amazon blocking personal agents and Shopify building a lane. It’s tempting to treat their moves as a test case, something to monitor from the sidelines until the winds blow in one definitive direction.

That would be a mistake. Sure, the headlines may change in a week; in the case of these specific AI agents and the companies that created them, there may be developments that complicate their rapid surge in the short term. But the shift is happening, and CX organizations can’t be lulled into a reactive posture.

Sources indicate that nobody has built the perfect system for this yet. But the companies spending this period of uncertainty getting their infrastructure ready will be the ones with real footing when the dust settles. Everyone else will still be reading the news, wondering what to do next.

#167697. Engineer, saleswoman, Elon Musk whisperer: Meet Gwynne Shotwell, the billionaire who really runs SpaceX

Engineer, saleswoman, Elon Musk whisperer: Meet Gwynne Shotwell, the billionaire who really runs SpaceX

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2002 Gwynne Shotwell had a lunch that would change her life—and the trajectory of the business world as we know it.
  • The owner, of course, was Elon Musk.
  • The investors and funds that have bought shares in SpaceX since its debut as, pre-Anthropic, the biggest IPO of all time are placing a huge bet on the visionary genius of Elon Musk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2002 Gwynne Shotwell had a lunch that would change her life—and the trajectory of the business world as we know it. Then 38, she had been working for a decade at a rocket startup, frustrated at the pace of innovation on the ground. “It wasn’t a vibrant industry, and we hadn’t gotten back to the moon [in 30 years],” she stated on a podcast in 2022. “The systems were designed to eliminate risk, so they took forever and cost too much.” A former colleague had just departed for another rocket startup, and she met him to celebrate at a favorite Austrian restaurant in the coastal L.A. suburb of El Segundo. Afterward, her friend suggested Shotwell stop by his new manufacturer to meet the owner.

The owner, of course, was Elon Musk. Fresh off making a fortune at PayPal, Musk laid out his vision to the curious Shotwell: make rockets a lot more cheaply than NASA; sell introduces to commercial satellite companies at super-bargain prices; slash prices even more by making the rockets reusable. Shotwell blurted out that he needed a “business developer,” effectively a sales leader who could win the pre-product contracts needed to fund the vision. Musk called her with an offer, and within days, Shotwell came aboard SpaceX. “I knew that working for Elon would be my last job in aerospace,” she has often noted.

The investors and funds that have bought shares in SpaceX since its debut as, pre-Anthropic, the biggest IPO of all time are placing a huge bet on the visionary genius of Elon Musk. Though they may not realize it, those investors are also betting on the far lesser-known figure who’s spent two decades at Musk’s side turning his seemingly crazy dreams into major-money ventures. Now 63, Shotwell was employee No. 7 at SpaceX, and the IPO made her extremely wealthy: her 12.6 million shares were worth some $2 billion after the tech giant went public. While Musk is SpaceX’s CEO, chairman, and chief technology officer (and controls around 40% of the shares), Shotwell’s the operator. As she put it in a recent interview, “He focuses on the future…on strategy and deep dives on the technical [side]. I focus on things that are helpful to customers today to earn money.” Shotwell doesn’t post on social media or seek publicity. She toils behind the scenes, mining Musk’s portfolio of futuristic ideas for the ones she can craft into cash-generating products.

Shotwell has achieved a spectacular record of tackling never-before-seen technological hurdles. She oversaw development of the Falcon 9, the world’s first orbital-class reusable commercial rocket, and helped make SpaceX the first private company to carry astronauts into orbit. Her cost breakthroughs enabled the Starlink galaxy of over 11,000 satellites, now SpaceX’s prime revenue and profit provider. Douglas Loverro, a former top official in the Air Force space program who’s worked extensively with Shotwell, told Fortune that for decades he’s believed that the only thing that makes money in space is communications and connectivity. “Elon and Gwynne saw it,” he observes. “Gwynne made it happen.”.

In a recent development, but Shotwell’s job just got exponentially more difficult. Musk has rebranded SpaceX as an AI company, taken it public, and forecast a $1 trillion revenue run rate by 2030, a feat he looks to achieve largely by putting data centers in orbit. To get there, SpaceX more than tripled its capex to $48.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026, and in August Shotwell unveiled a $100 billion Louisiana launch site to send them up. Skeptics, including some who won’t bet against Musk, doubt the economics can ever work. The numbers, observes Aswath Damodaran, a professor at NYU’s Stern School of Business, are “mind-blowingly large.” His biggest fear for SpaceX’s future is that “it overspends on orbital AI.”.

Sources indicate that the biggest thing working in Shotwell’s favor is that she has mastered a challenge that has defeated many others: managing Musk himself. As Walter Isaacson states in his definitive biography Elon Musk, the boss “doesn’t naturally partner with people. Collegiality is not part of his skill set. He inspires, frightens, bullies, and does not like to share power.” At Tesla, for example, Musk named one president who served just over two years, and never replaced him. Somehow, Shotwell’s rare combination of an engineering mindset, a knack for smoothly wooing customers, not to mention her money-making instincts, has fully captured Musk’s confidence.

According to recent reports, people who’ve observed the pair in action credit Shotwell as the adult in the next cubicle. “I’ve worked with both Elon and Gwynne, and I’ve got to tell you, working with Gwynne is a lot more pleasant,” says one former client. As Isaacson told Fortune, “Gwynne’s indispensable to SpaceX, a perfect mind partner for Elon. She knows how to accomplish his goals while occasionally altering his trajectories and being engineering-honest with him, which is the way he likes to operate. She combines an engineering mind with a fingertip feel for how to deal with people.”.

It’s a kind of odd-couple collaboration that works. Tom Mueller, SpaceX’s first employee and developer of the Merlin engine that powers the Falcon rockets, mentioned in an email to Fortune that Shotwell brought a “unique skillset to the table that complements all the talent Elon was assembling.” In other interviews Mueller, who retired from SpaceX in 2020, put it even more simply: “I built the rockets, but Gwynne built the company.”.

Sources indicate that for 24 years Musk has supplied the vision, and Shotwell’s genius has been finding the money. Now she has to monetize the most expensive idea he’s ever had. The question is, Can she? Can anyone?

In her own way, Shotwell’s just as much a Big Personality as Elon Musk. Regularly attired in dark blazers, skinny jeans and super-high heels, sporting a flowing blond coif and typically, a crescent of pearls, she’s a born raconteur who describes herself as “a people engineer.” Today she and her husband, Robert Shotwell, a NASA engineer, are repurposing their ranch on the San Gabriel River in Texas as a vineyard. From the spread, Gwynne drives to work in a bright red Tesla Model S, a Starlink mini-dish strapped to the ski rack so she doesn’t drop the call when Elon phones.

Sources indicate that for this story, SpaceX declined to make Shotwell available for interviews. She’s talked extensively to the mainstream or business media only a few times, though over the past 20 years she has spoken in depth to industry groups and at universities, including her alma mater Northwestern. Where not otherwise attributed, Fortune’s account of her background and career draws on those public statements and on Isaacson’s Elon Musk.

Gwynne Rowley grew up in the Chicago suburb of Libertyville, the middle daughter of an artist mom and a father who taught neurosurgery at Northwestern medical school. She relished fixing bicycles, but her career-sparking revelation came when her mother dragged the 15-year-old to a conference for the Society of Women Engineers. “I didn’t want to be there, I was a grumpy teenager,” Shotwell recalls. “I was interested in cheerleading and clothes. I thought of engineers as nerds and outcasts.”.

In a recent development, but one mechanical engineer’s super-style black suit and elegant footwear knocked Gwynne out. “I went up and congratulated her on her suit,” says Shotwell. Suddenly, she decided engineers could be “cool.” But Shotwell doesn’t discount her glamorous high school avocation as training for the business world. “Cheerleaders make great salespeople,” she observes.

It has been revealed that in 1986, Shotwell was one of three women in her class of 36 who graduated from Northwestern’s McCormick School of Engineering. Two years later, she joined Aerospace Corp., a nonprofit that advises government and commercial space programs, where she wrote papers modeling how heated and cooled satellite components work in tandem—a challenge that’s paramount for orbital data centers. But her real passion was designing and building spacecraft. So after 10 years, she joined Microcosm Inc., which won military and NASA contracts to architect rockets aimed at radically reducing the cost of sending satellites into space.

Then came the fateful lunch and meeting with Elon.

Shotwell’s mission: Selling contracts to military and corporate clients to fund development of the lowest-cost rocket ever produced. “If you don’t have a rocket to sell, what’s really important is selling the team,” recalls Shotwell. “Selling the technical savvy of your CEO and making sure you can address any technical issue right away.” Shotwell worked out of a cubicle next to Musk’s, and would even vacuum the conference room prior to client meetings. As Mueller told Fortune, “We were writing our own playbook across all aspects of the business, and she jumped in and became a contributor from day one.”.

In a recent development, indeed, Shotwell won clients for the maiden SpaceX launches from an atoll in the South Pacific, aboard its new Falcon 1 rocket, including NASA and the DOD. On the first three flights, the rockets either failed or exploded. Musk believed SpaceX had sufficient cash for two more attempts; Shotwell told Musk that he was being a Pollyanna, and that if the next one flopped, SpaceX would flame out, too. On the fourth liftoff day in September of 2008, Shotwell was in a hotel in Glasgow apologizing to customers who’d lost payloads on the earlier launches when, well past midnight, she watched the livestream of the Falcon 1 reaching orbit and carrying a dummy payload nicknamed RatSat that substituted for a satellite the Malaysian government pulled due to nervousness over the three failed flights. She relishes telling how she ran down the hotel corridor in her “jammies” yelling joyously, and commandeered the bar for a night of champagne and revelry.

It has been revealed that “I built the rockets, but Gwynne built the manufacturer. We were writing our own playbook.“.

Industry observers note that that first successful launch landed SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract from NASA to deliver cargo to the International Space Station. The deal also inspired Musk to offer her the position of president at the close of 2008. She relates that at first, she “thought it was weird to be boss” and “my first reaction was ‘no.’” But after “a nanosecond of stupidity,” she noted yes to Musk. Since then, SpaceX has made 36 cargo and 14 crewed introduces to the ISS for NASA, long its biggest customer. In 2010, SpaceX introduced the Falcon 1’s successor, the 21-story-tall Falcon 9 that’s still its workhorse.

It has been revealed that shotwell’s a whiz at deploying templates to drive down costs. Instead of paying what she claims would have been $1 billion to develop an all-upcoming engine for the Falcon 9, SpaceX packed nine of the Falcon 1’s Merlins into the booster; Starship, which will head its future fleets, carries a total of 39 Raptor engines developed in-house. Other solutions look improvised: Isaacson relates that, faced with an estimated cost of more than $3 million for Falcon 9’s payload-bay cooling system, SpaceX instead bought and modified commercial air-conditioning units priced at a few thousand each.

According to recent reports, shotwell also brings an intangible asset that’s essential to SpaceX’s rise: superb diplomatic skills. Loverro has marveled for two decades at how she maintains lucrative relationships after tough client encounters that could have closed the door. “Back in 2007, we were relying on America’s only rocket company that was charging ridiculous prices,” he told Fortune. Loverro negotiated with Shotwell for a year to launch a battlefield imaging satellite on the Falcon 1, and SpaceX won the bid. “Just when I was about to tell her she’d won, Gwynne calls to tell me they were shutting down Falcon 1 production.”.

Sources indicate that loverro took plenty of flak from the Air Force brass, but remained convinced that Shotwell could deliver. A couple of years later, Congress committed $50 million for an experimental satellite launch that the Air Force feared would cost more. “I asked Gwynne, ‘Are you able to do it for $50 million?’ and she said yes, for that fixed price. Fixed prices were their specialty.”.

The successful launch happened in 2015. “SpaceX was four years late, but they’re always late,” notes Loverro. Even after Musk famously sued the U.S. Air Force for awarding contracts to a rival sans competitive bids, government business kept flowing to SpaceX, and Loverro awards much of the credit to Shotwell. “Imagine your firm is suing the government, but someone has to do business with the government anyway! That was Gwynne.”.

Sources indicate that shotwell can even do something that many have deemed impossible: Get Musk to change his mind. Isaacson relates that in 2019, Musk impulsively decided to shutter the Falcon Heavy. Shotwell sped to his cubicle, reminded Musk that SpaceX needed its then-biggest vehicle to fulfill a major military contract, and got him to nix the cancellation. According to the biography, she also denounced Musk’s promise to award the Pentagon free use of SpaceX internet service to his face as “ridiculous,” and made sure Starlink got paid. In interviews, she proudly describes herself as blunt and “mouthy,” and according to Isaacson, skewers longtime lieutenants who won’t stand up to Musk, calling them “chickens.”.

Still, Shotwell’s in many ways just as tough a boss as Musk. She admits that Musk “does create uncomfortable situations in the office,” and though her style’s far more agreeable, Shotwell is apparently brutal in demanding that employees strive to achieve his super-elastic goals. “‘We can’t do that’ is not in SpaceX’s lexicon,” she likes to intone. “I’m not a tech developer, but it’s my job to figure out how to do all these crazy things, and if you think ‘there’s no way we’re doing that,’ you zip it, you think about it, and you find ways to get it done.”.

In fact, Shotwell mirrors the boss’s wishes by running just about the most demanding workplace on earth. “One year at SpaceX is like 10 anywhere else. There’s no boundary between work and life outside of work,” Branden Spikes, SpaceX’s CIO for nearly 10 years, told Fortune. Musk has noted that if 10% of employees aren’t leaving each year, his companies aren’t running at maximum efficiency.

It has been revealed that shotwell echoes that approach, in a nicer way. “We ‘counsel out’ about 10% of employees each year,” she notes. “If you don’t like continuous feedback, if you don’t like running a marathon, if you want to walk a marathon, you don’t want to work at SpaceX.”.

Recent findings suggest that shotwell’s behind-the-scenes, find-the-dollars pragmatism allowed SpaceX to take daredevil chances that delivered. But now, Shotwell’s the steward of a public firm, and she’s showing her pragmatism by publicly tempering some of her boss’s more outrageous forecasts. Musk predicts in typical style that Starlink will multiply its broadband universe to 100,000 satellites in five years. In a good sign of caution, Shotwell puts the number at 12,000 to 15,000, keeping in mind that its new V3 models are far more powerful than their predecessors.

SpaceX now comprises three main businesses: “Space,” or the launch arm; the Starlink satellite franchise plus the fledgling Starlink Mobile, grouped as “Connectivity” in its financial reports; and AI, now called Super Intelligence (SI), comprising terrestrial data campuses, inherited from xAI, and the forthcoming Starmind orbital AI data centers, which unite xAI’s expertise with Starship’s capacity to launch giant satellites that bring compute to space.

In broadband satellite and launch, Musk and Shotwell have built one of the deepest moats in tech. SpaceX’s Space segment is “a decade-plus ahead of any competitor,” Julie Zhu, an analyst at MoffettNathanson, wrote in a recent report. Starlink accounts for three-quarters of all the broadband birds in orbit, and last year SpaceX flew 165 orbital missions, 85% of the U.S. and half the world total.

SpaceX is also pushing hard in terrestrial data centers. The former xAI built the first phase of a giant facility called Colossus 1 in just 120 days in 2024; the campus now covers 200 acres in the Memphis area, and its Colossus 2 claims the title of the world’s largest data center. Led by the Colossus expansion, SpaceX vows to grow its capacity more than fourfold to 13 gigawatts by the close of next year, adding in around a year and a half what Google built in its entire existence.

Colossus was first built primarily to run the Grok chatbot, which never caught the leader group of Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini. But Musk had shrewdly filled the facilities with Nvidia GPUs and other advanced chips now in short supply, and starting in May, he and Shotwell began leasing space to rivals famished for capacity. Deals with Google, Anthropic, Reflection AI and a fourth, undisclosed major player generate an incredible $3.4 billion a month in revenue. Renters can cancel at the end of a 90-day period, which helps explain the extremely high rates, but if the AI capex boom continues, the earth-based campuses should prove strongly profitable for years. Zhu predicts that the terrestrial group will supply the highest revenues of the four sectors, reaching $102 billion by 2031, 40% of the SpaceX total.

Recent findings suggest that musk and Shotwell, however, are counting on a totally unproven horizon in AI as the primary force in making SpaceX the world’s biggest and most profitable enterprise in a matter of years. At first look—and the way the pair characterize them—orbital AI data centers look far superior to their terrestrial counterparts, at least once SpaceX tames the launching costs, always a top strength.

Industry observers note that shotwell sketches that celestial image just as enthusiastically as her boss. During a CNBC interview in June, she argued that “the most efficient place for AI compute is in space,” and backed that “space is better” scenario at the All-In Summit tech conference in mid-September. On a panel, she cited that terrestrial campuses face long lag times for permits, licensing, and power supplies, and that land costs are enormous, avowing that “when someone finds out supercompute is going in, real estate goes from $3,000 to $180,000 an acre.” Yet, she added, “People need compute now.” Orbital centers will immensely speed the process, she maintained. “The real estate in space is infinite. And it’s free,” declared Shotwell; she also stressed that SpaceX can supply everything in house from the giant fresh Starship that will carry the loads to custom-manufacturing for the AI birds, which she says are “much simpler” than the V3 satellites. She even did something seldom witnessed at SpaceX: advanced the timing, forecasting that the AI satellites will fly into low-earth orbit next year, up from the pre-IPO target of 2028.

Recent findings suggest that besides providing the compute much quicker, the AI data centers, Shotwell and Musk argue, should be far cheaper. The reason: Power and cooling account for as much as 70% of a data center’s operating costs, and Musk and Shotwell argue correctly that plants in orbit pay nothing in direct expense for electricity or for keeping chips at an optimal temperature. “Deep space is the coldest thing out there,” Shotwell said at the All-In event. Yet all major studies now show that with current technology, orbital centers would cost a lot more all-in than the big boxes in Loudoun County, Va., or outside Memphis. Andrew McCalip, head of research at Varda Space Industries, reckons that running a 1 GW facility in orbit would cost $51.1 billion for the first five years, against $15.9 billion for the terrestrial equivalent.

In a recent development, put simply, orbital centers trade much lower operating costs for far higher upfront expense for equipment, the heavy charges for lifting it into space, and most of all, a shorter life. Heating and cooling in space also aren’t “free.” Space has no atmosphere, so chips can’t be cooled by air or water as on earth; a modest-sized 100 MW data center requires a cluster of some 700 satellites, each carrying big radiators and solar panels. Each would feature 1,200-square-foot radiators, equal in size to one-and-a-half pickleball courts.

According to recent reports, A major reason for the three-to-one cost differential: lifting each unit, with its 231-foot wingspan, into orbit. Today, SpaceX estimates its launch costs at around $2,700 per kg, and Shotwell and Musk pledge to crush that number to under $200 in a couple of years, on the way to below $100. Their significant ace, besides Starship, is the Louisiana site that will be the world’s largest spaceport. By 2035, Adam Jonas of Morgan Stanley predicts, seven flights a day—and likely far more—will depart on Starship from four sites, most of the debuts from the Louisiana coast. But slaying the launch-cost dragon isn’t enough, according to experts Fortune interviewed. Radiation gradually degrades the radiators and solar panels, causing them to lose potency over time. Earthbound facilities experience annualized failure rates of 3% to 5% for their equipment, but mechanics can replace the faulty units in minutes. No robot repair crews exist in space, and building them would hugely add to costs. The chips must also be space-hardened, which Nvidia is developing specifically for SpaceX, while its Terafab joint venture with Intel and Tesla works on custom orbital semiconductors.

Recent findings suggest that data centers in space also have an estimated life of just five years, while on earth the buildings, cooling, and power systems function far longer. That, plus gradually declining power and no way to fix parts gone bad, will make it extremely tough for orbital centers to compete with the giant campuses on earth.

Notes a top executive in the data center industry, “My overall conclusion is that these are very difficult technical challenges. I just don’t see the problem it’s solving. … If you can develop chips that run far hotter for space and produce more power, why not use them on earth? We have a power grid on earth.”.

But this titan also cautions, “Elon’s record is significant. I’m not sure I’d bet for it, but I’m also not ready to bet against it.” Several sources interviewed by Fortune believe that orbital data centers’ best prospects are as “escape valves” that offer needed capacity if the backlash against terrestrial campuses takes hold long-term. That’s conceivable, but hardly a highly investable scenario.

Industry observers note that technical issues pose a big barrier, and so does money. Overall, Wall Street was projecting the biggest capex blowout in corporate history before the Q2 surprise and announcement of the epic project in Louisiana. Jonas is typical among the analysts in positing that SpaceX won’t begin to see significant sales from Musk’s brainchild until at least 2032. Though Morgan Stanley posits that the campaign will eventually be a big winner, the timeline to getting there spotlights the difficulty. It predicts that SpaceX will burn cash through 2030, and require $390 billion in debt financing through that date to help fund its gigantic capex spend over the next eight to nine years.

In a recent development, as Morgan Stanley and other banks highlight, SpaceX can dial back on capex if the prospects for AI in space start looking dim. But as Shotwell acknowledges, SpaceX almost never delivers on time, and for years to come it may wrestle with the fresh technologies needed to make orbital compute profitable, without a clear line of sight to when, or if, that will happen. Meanwhile, heavy spending subsidized by Starlink could hammer overall earnings, and a share price elevated largely by great expectations for SpaceX’s galaxies of compute in low-earth orbit.

Recent findings suggest that shotwell has spent two decades proving the skeptics wrong, over and over. This time she’s facing engineering hurdles that even executives unwilling to bet against Musk call very difficult, at a price tag in capex that Wall Street already rates as the biggest in the annals of big business. If anyone can find the money in Musk’s latest moonshot, it’s Shotwell. The harder question for SpaceX shareholders is what happens if he insists on chasing a dream and, for once, she can’t stop him.

  • This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.
  • With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue shows that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The XRP ETF market might be bracing to close a record-breaking month of outflows as demand for the XRP-based investment product has remained on hold all through the month.

This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.

With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue shows that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.

Previous ETF data highlights that March remains the only month in which spot XRP ETFs have recorded net outflows since their launch.

While it still stands as the record outflow month for XRP ETFs, investors withdrew about $31.16 million from the funds during that month.

This means that the persistent withdrawals seen this month have brought the November outflow dangerously close to its previous monthly record seen in March.

Apparently, the spot XRP ETFs are on track to close November as their worst-performing month since launch, with just about $1 million left to hit the record.

Further data also highlights that the spot XRP ETFs have yet to record a single day of net inflows throughout November, as the persistent price decline has caused investors to slow down their purchases.

As such, the influx of fresh capital into the spot XRP ETF market has remained on hold amid growing market uncertainty and a shift in investor sentiment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors.
  • It has been revealed that the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.

Amazon and Fresh York City are fighting again.

Recent findings suggest that the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

It has been revealed that the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

It has been revealed that companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

Sources indicate that on Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon noted it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the tech giant wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

Amazon released its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

Industry observers note that in a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the organization works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The firm also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

In a recent development, the standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the manufacturer abruptly canceled looks to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Upcoming Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6.

In a recent development, city leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

It has been revealed that amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company mentioned it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in Fresh York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you’re like me, your approach to nutrition mostly involves squinting at a label, not recognizing any of the ingredients, and eating the thing anyway. Peter Castleman decided that wasn’t good enough. After four decades as an investor, including as Chairman and Managing Partner of J.H. Whitney & Co., where he played a role in investments tied to The North Face, Igloo and Herbalife, Peter came out of retirement to become the founder and CEO of WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform that has mapped more than 840,000 products. He’s 70 years old and says he’s never felt more excited about an idea, proving it’s never too late to chase a major idea.

Give us the elevator pitch. What is WISEcode?Basically, we’re trying to solve what I call the food information crisis. We literally don’t know two things: what’s in our food and what it does to us. At WISEcode, we’ve been spending a dozen years or so solving that. We’ve created what we call the Food Genome Project, which is really mapping the entire food system. So we now know exactly what’s in our foods, and we can tell you what it does for you. And that applies to consumers, policymakers, government people, industries, retailers, scientists, everyone. That information didn’t exist, and now it does.

This isn’t the first firm you’ve started or been a big part of. Why did you want to become a founder again?Well, I’m 70, okay? When I turned 50, I retired from my firm. I’m healthy. I eat generally well. But when you turn 50, you enter the kill zone for chronic disease, and chronic disease is 90% of our health issues, and 80% of chronic disease is driven by what we choose to do. We actually control most of our health outcomes. So I basically wanted to simply hack what I’m going to eat. I didn’t want to get cognitive issues. I didn’t want to get any late-onset chronic disease. But that hack doesn’t exist. It shocked me. It just doesn’t exist. So this passion became the business purpose of WISEcode, and I mentioned, “Okay, I’m gonna get this information. I’m going to do for me, I’m going to do for every single individual. I’m going to give them Food Truth.” Formally, I’ve probably been doing this for about 12, 13 years. Informally, I’ve been thinking about it for 20 years.

Industry observers note that when a business is a personal passion, do you have a process for figuring out whether it will be a passion for other people, too? Or do you just follow your heart?Like many people, I suffer from that latter part, which is letting your emotions get too far into stuff. I’ve always stated, “Fall in love with your family and your friends, not your businesses.” It’s hard to do, because you develop passions. I have three tests I generally apply to any kind of activity. The first I call the North Star test: is it very clear that what you’re trying to do resonates with others? Is it going to be an aha moment or a so-what moment to the world? Number two, I call the sandbox test. How massive is your sandbox? How big is your addressable market? And how crowded is your sandbox? And then the third one I call the moat test, which is: can you build defensible business assets that prevent people from copying what you do? People will copy you in a second if you’re successful. If I’m not slam-dunk strong on all three tests, I try to stay away. I apply that to WISEcode. I apply it to everything I do. I’m better at it now than I was at 25.

How do you figure out if other people are interested in your idea when you don’t have a big budget?Social media and everything we have today are double-edged swords. But I use SurveyMonkey all the time. You can ask a question and, for not very much money, you can get 500, 1,000 really clear answers that help you evolve. You can do the same thing on social media tools. The tools out there today are so great. It used to be you’d have to hire McKinsey or Bain for a gazillion dollars, and they’d do a six-month study. Now, in a day, you can get better information than they ever gave you.

Sources indicate that what do you say to someone in their 50s who thinks, “I always wanted to do my own thing, but it’s too late”?First and foremost, I think you gotta be honest with yourself. Who are you? What do you love doing, and are you good at this? Late in your career, any time, if you don’t have the energy, the drive and the staying power, don’t do it. Because building companies is hard. You’re going to get knocked on your fanny a ton of times. You gotta get back up. You gotta inspire others around you. You gotta keep going when everyone says, “Don’t do it.” You’re gonna run out of money. You’re gonna have your spouse saying, “What the hell are you doing?” But if it’s in your DNA, it’s the greatest thing in the world. Most of my contemporaries are reducing their handicap on the golf course, and I’m spending 10 hours a day, seven days a week on WISEcode, and I love it. I wouldn’t change it for the world, but that’s me. The greatest joy I get, besides my love of my friends and family, is building businesses that actually make a difference, and if that’s in your DNA, do it. I think the only failure in life is not trying.

#167693. On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years.
  • Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first.
  • In a recent development, although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years. January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement. The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services confirmed on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

In a recent development, although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

Recent findings suggest that for a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay the standard premium out of their benefits. Higher-income enrollees pay income-based surcharges on top of it, while states cover the Part B premium for about one in five Medicare enrollees with low incomes and savings.

Industry observers note that by recent standards, this year’s hike is mild. The 3.2% premium increase is smaller than the COLA for the first time since 2023; in 2026, the premium jumped 9.7% against a 2.8% COLA.

Sources indicate that even though COLAs are treated like bonuses or raises, they’re not. As David Herbert, director of economics & economic freedom and a senior research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER), told The Hill, “It’s meant to make sure that Social Security recipients are receiving the same amount of spending power as they did in the past. It’s not actually going to make them wealthier or have an easier time buying things that they weren’t already going to buy.”.

Sources indicate that seniors appear to agree. In an AARP survey conducted before the announcement, 80% of Social Security recipients mentioned a projected 3.5% COLA in 2027 would not keep up with rising prices. When the final number landed, some retirees dismissed it as too little to offset soaring costs.

It has been revealed that it seems as though seniors are right. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 3.7% annual inflation for September 2026, its most recent annual figure. The 3.6% COLA will not keep up, especially since the higher payments don’t start until January.

By then, seniors will have absorbed higher prices since March, when inflation hit 3.3% and outpaced the 2026 COLA of 2.8%. It peaked at 4.2% in May. In other words, a 3.6% COLA is a small improvement, but it comes too late.

Recent findings suggest that against the backdrop of higher benefits and costs looms Social Security’s insolvency. The 2026 Trustees Report found that starting in the fourth quarter of 2032, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will no longer be able to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. Instead, recipients would receive only 78% of them.

Sources indicate that part of the funding shortfall comes down to demographics. According to the trustees’ projections, about 2.6 workers paid in for every beneficiary in 2025, compared with 41.9 in 1945. The trustees expect the ratio to keep falling, to about 1.9 workers per beneficiary by 2075.

With fewer workers paying into Social Security, “Congress is going to have to step in and do something,” said Herbert. “What is going to be left over for people who are not quite at retirement but are hoping at some point to see any form of a return on investment on this money that we’ve been sending the federal government for our entire working lives?”.

That job falls to the latest Congress, which convenes in January and has roughly six years to act before automatic cuts kick in. In the meantime, Herbert advises those a decade or two from retirement to start saving and investing. More importantly, workers shouldn’t plan on receiving full Social Security benefits in retirement.

Tech Report: Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • The most crucial words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

The most crucial words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

Sources indicate that it also remarked it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

In a recent development, early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

Sources indicate that the staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

Recent findings suggest that that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

Recent findings suggest that this is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

Sources indicate that the second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the challenges presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

It has been revealed that in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

According to recent reports, for a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

Recent findings suggest that that sequence matters. The interpretation indicates what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

Industry observers note that the harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

It has been revealed that for now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

Industry News: I Stayed On a Private Island in Fiji. It Pulls Off a Top Travel Trend With a Luxury Twist—Here’s What Any Hospitality Business Can Learn.

💡 Key Takeaways
