📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Lang Walker, the late Australian billionaire property developer and philanthropist, and his wife, Sue Walker, first saw Yaukuve Levu Island, Kadavu, Fiji, surrounded by the Great Astrolabe Reef, the land was largely overgrown, with the remains of a development that had never been completed.

Sources indicate that “We anchored the boat out the front, looked at it and thought what a wonderful place this could be,” Sue Walker recalls. “It took eight years and an enormous amount of hard work to bring that vision to life.”.

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

Today, the property features 21 beachfront villas and five hilltop residences, each with a private pool; three principal dining venues, with more than 80% of herbs and greens sourced from the island’s 5.5-acre organic farm; the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with its dedicated fitness center; and no shortage of adventure and cultural activities available to its guests.

My husband and I had a chance to experience the tropical island paradise for ourselves in September. Throughout our stay, we were struck by Kokomo’s sheer natural beauty and how much the luxury hospitality experience was rooted in a genuine sense of place.

It has been revealed that increasingly, hotels and resorts highlighting local character rise to the top of travelers’ wishlists. Nearly three-quarters of luxury travelers won’t pay for accommodations that feel generic, per a report from Preferred Hotels & Resorts, and 77% of travelers prioritize authentic experiences representative of local culture, according to research from Booking.com.

Industry observers note that kokomo serves as a lesson in hospitality excellence — what it takes to succeed in a travel landscape increasingly defined by a desire for authenticity and local character. Here’s how every business can do the same.

Sources indicate that after a long day (or more) of travel, first impressions are key. Guests want to feel at ease and an immediate sense of place. But, sometimes, that’s the straightforward part. Sustaining that genuine warm welcome throughout the stay also matters.

Staff members at Kokomo give it its personality and make guests feel at home, often forming relationships that bring people back year after year, Walker says.

Additionally, Kokomo has developed a close relationship with the local community, where some staff members are from: supporting local employment, working with neighboring villages, and contributing to education, healthcare and community initiatives.

“Authenticity comes from allowing those relationships and traditions to exist naturally, rather than trying to manufacture an experience for guests,” Walker says. “When someone shares a story about their village, introduces a guest to a local custom or folklore or even simply welcomes them with genuine Fijian hospitality, that’s what stays with people.”.

It has been revealed that our arrival and journey to Kokomo was seamless from the first “bula” (Fijian for “hello” and a wish for life and good health). After a 45-minute seaplane ride, we touched down on the crystalline blue waters in front of Kokomo. We were given a salusalu, a traditional garland worn around the neck, and coconut water, and listened to a group of staff members sing traditional Fijian welcome songs.

Industry observers note that that warmth and hospitality extended throughout our time at Kokomo, across the interactions we had with staff and when we visited the nearby Dravuni Village, which is home to a small indigenous Fijian community. We heard traditional songs, learned about their hand-woven crafts, participated in a kava ceremony and toured the village with a staff member who’d grown up there.

The business lesson is this: Lean into what makes a destination special, and the cultural touchstones that define it, for an authentic welcome that extends from the first moment to the last.

It has been revealed that of course, as much as people want to soak up all a destination has to offer, they’ll spend a good portion of their vacation in their accommodations. Ideally, those accommodations capture the destination’s unique characteristics while prioritizing comfort.

From the beginning, the Walkers wanted Kokomo to feel like home, “albeit a rather extraordinary one,” where families could create lifelong memories with the privacy, space and luxury afforded by their own quiet corner of the island.

Industry observers note that “For me, true luxury isn’t about formality,” Walker states. “It’s about comfort, freedom, being able to enjoy yourself without feeling constrained by the usual expectations of a hotel. Children should be able to run around, explore and have adventures, while their parents and grandparents can relax and enjoy the island in their own way.”.

Our one-bedroom beachfront villa, just steps from the ocean, felt sprung from the tropical landscape itself. The high ceilings, neutral stone and wood, and ample windows, the better to display the expansive patio with its private pool and the dazzling ocean view, created an indoor-outdoor flow with understated natural elegance.

When it comes to architecture, interior design, or landscape, embracing what sets the place surrounding it apart from any other, rather than competing with it, helps establish that seamless, one-of-kind experience guests won’t forget.

Whether a guest is a serious gourmet or not, meals will stand out as part of the experience (a three-times-a-day touchpoint). For remote resorts where guests rely solely on the dining on-site, it’s even more critical to deliver elevated, locally-defined experiences.

Early on, the Walkers realized they had access to the best ingredients on their doorstep — fresh seafood and the climate and space to grow much of the island’s own produce — and built their culinary philosophy around that, Walker states.

In a recent development, “A fish caught locally that morning, vegetables picked from the garden, herbs cut just before they’re used,” she explains. “You can’t get much fresher than that. Building and operating a resort in such a remote location comes with enormous logistical challenges, so growing more of our own food and reducing our reliance on imported produce makes sense on many levels.”.

We had a chance to go on a tour with Kokomo’s executive chef Marty Kindleysides. He gave us an inside look at the island’s farm and hydroponic gardens, which help shape the menus across its restaurants: the Beach Shack on Kokomo’s western beach; Walker D’Plank, featuring Asian-influenced cuisine, near the arrival jetty; and the poolside Kokocabana, highlighting Italian-inspired dishes.

From the beautiful lunch Kindleysides prepared for us with farm-fresh ingredients like squash and kale, to all of the meals we enjoyed at the other dining venues, including a showstopping dinner by Chef Caroline during a curry-themed night at Walker D’Plank, the food was flavorful, intentional and reinforced a singular dining experience.

Guests should never feel like the food where they’re staying is an afterthought; it’s another opportunity — and a very memorable one — to showcase innovation and what makes a setting unique.

In a recent development, at a remote tropical resort like Kokomo, guests have the luxury of a picture-perfect natural setting offering once-in-a-lifetime activities. But striking the balance between making the most of the environment and protecting it is also critical.

According to recent reports, lang was an avid diver for most of his life and immediately recognized the wonder of the Great Astrolabe Reef. The Walkers saw it as their responsibility to look after it, so they set out to help guests experience and understand it.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s something quite powerful about a child helping to plant coral, or a family learning about the individual manta rays that return to our waterways each season,” Walker indicates. “Suddenly conservation becomes personal. You’re no longer looking at a beautiful reef, rather, you’re beginning to understand how it works and why protecting it matters.”.

Sources indicate that we had the opportunity to meet with a marine biologist to learn about the manta rays and conservation efforts. Kokomo has partnered with Manta Project Fiji to research and protect Fiji’s reef manta rays since 2017. More than 500 manta ray sightings were recorded during the most recent monitoring period. We even went to look for them by boat, but unfortunately with it being the tail end of the season, didn’t spot any.

Sources indicate that additionally, the marine biologist led us on a guided coral restoration tour, where we snorkeled over some of the current projects underway. More than 2,000 corals have been transplanted as part of Kokomo’s coral restoration. The island also has six active coral nurseries, which can support more than 10,000 corals per season.

Bringing guests into the very projects that protect the place they’re staying gives them destination-driven, extraordinary experiences while safeguarding them for future generations.

Relaxation means different things to different people, but centralizing spa and wellness options in one place, and melding personalized comfort with distinct ambiance, gives everyone the option to design an ideal routine to reset.

The Walkers wanted to build on the feeling guests have upon arrival — everyday life demands removed by the grandeur of nature — and developed the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with that in mind.

“The gardens, the tropical landscape, the sense of privacy all contribute to the experience,” Walker indicates. “I wanted guests to feel that they could completely switch off, even if only for an hour or two. I don’t think wellness needs to be complicated or overly prescriptive. Sometimes the greatest luxury is having the time and space to do what makes you feel good, without the schedule or expectation.”.

Sources indicate that we enjoyed Kokomo’s signature “Pacific Mastery Massage,” which incorporates centuries-old methods from traditional Fijian Bobo, combining variable pressure and rhythmic movement with the preferred oil blend. Before and after the service, we sipped iced hibiscus tea (the flower is often seen in Fijian landscaping) in the garden setting.

Recent findings suggest that guests will remember how a vacation makes them feel, so making sure they have the option to truly unwind, whatever that looks like for them, is key. Infusing it with a local twist means they won’t forget exactly where they experienced it.

At the end of the stay, as we departed on the one-hour helicopter ride back to the hangar, spotting our villa on the lush island encircled by a shock of turquoise, we came away already nostalgic for the trip, and with a deeper appreciation for Fiji’s natural beauty and vibrant culture.

We would love to return some day (maybe to snorkel with the mantas) — and that’s exactly what the Walkers intended.

It has been revealed that “More than anything, I hope guests leave Kokomo feeling they’ve been part of something special,” Walker says. “That they’ve spent quality time with the people they love, experienced the generosity of our Fijian team and discovered a part of the world they’ll always remember. If they leave feeling as though Kokomo is their island home, then we’ve achieved what we set out to do.”.

When Lang Walker, the late Australian billionaire property developer and philanthropist, and his wife, Sue Walker, first saw Yaukuve Levu Island, Kadavu, Fiji, surrounded by the Great Astrolabe Reef, the land was largely overgrown, with the remains of a development that had never been completed.

“We anchored the boat out the front, looked at it and thought what a wonderful place this could be,” Sue Walker recalls. “It took eight years and an enormous amount of hard work to bring that vision to life.”.

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has unveiled a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the tech giant’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

Recent findings suggest that in August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals revealed a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”.

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

Recent findings suggest that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to an estimated $120 million in North America this weekend, nearly three times the $44 million debut of its 2023 predecessor, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. The Lionsgate prequel added $105 million overseas for a $225 million global launch, returning the franchise to the three-figure heights of its original run.

In a recent development, it did so in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited Rockstar Games release that arrived one day earlier. Fans and industry insiders alike speculated that the game, which topped $1 billion in pre-sales ahead of its Nov. 19 launch, would monopolize the attention economy and drain an already thin November box office.

Sources indicate that in hindsight, releasing a Hunger Games movie the day after GTA VI may have been a clever piece of counterprogramming. “I think the marketplace has already spoken,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian told the Associated Press.

It has been revealed that both GTA and The Hunger Games are now multigenerational action franchises, but the former has always targeted men, mostly young-adult to 40-year-old gamers drawn to its edgy depictions of criminal violence. The Hunger Games, meanwhile, has its roots in teen readers and women.

According to recent reports, like the five films before it, Sunrise on the Reaping is adapted from Suzanne Collins’ young-adult novels. It centers on 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, played by Joseph Zada, but the series was built around its heroine, Katniss Everdeen. Jennifer Lawrence, who led the original four films as Katniss, returns for a brief epilogue cameo.

The opening-weekend audience bears out the split. Women made up 67% of ticket buyers and 74% were between 18 and 34, according to the AP. Lionsgate studied the risks of opening against GTA from the earliest stage of dating the film and concluded the two could coexist.

While the Mature-rated GTA VI may have kept men of a certain age glued to their consoles this weekend, the PG-13 Sunrise on the Reaping held onto the core Hunger Games crowd: young women, along with teens too young to play the game.

Sources indicate that that base may also have come out of thirst for a big-screen, four-quadrant blockbuster. This fall has been a sleepy season for PG-13 action movies, with dramas, documentaries, and R-rated fare dominating the box office and the zeitgeist. Audiences liked what they found: the film earned an A- CinemaScore, up from the B+ that greeted Songbirds & Snakes.

It has been revealed that overall, the weekend was a surprisingly strong one for theaters. Total domestic grosses topped $160 million, nearly double the prior weekend, though still about 10% below the same frame last year, when Wicked: For Good opened.

Sunrise on the Reaping accounted for most of that. Behind it on the weekend chart came I Play Rocky with $9.3 million in its first weekend of wide release, Ebenezer at $7.7 million, and The Cat in the Hat at $6.9 million. You Can See Everything is still hanging in the top 10, adding another $2.5 million.

Recent findings suggest that these titles are diverse, but most target an audience different from GTA VI. Beyond The Hunger Games locking up young women, I Play Rocky is for the boomer dads and The Cat in the Hat is for kids.

None of it came close to GTA VI. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent firm, says the game’s day-one retail sales, including preorders, reached $3.79 billion worldwide, more than 20 times the weekend’s entire domestic box office.

Still, Hollywood held its own heading into Thanksgiving week, suggesting that with the right strategy, audiences will still show up for the movies, and that GTA VI may not dominate every corner of the entertainment economy this season. The next test comes this weekend, when Sunrise on the Reaping faces a crowded holiday slate that includes Disney’s animated Hexed.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am.

Orchard Robotics, an agtech organization using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was revealed Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

In a recent development, the startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, noted in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

It has been revealed that “Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Recent findings suggest that orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round revealed in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

Recent findings suggest that the Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

Why Xi’s brief APEC handshake with Takaichi reflects a frozen China-Japan relationship

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi shook hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen last week, the closest thing to a thaw in China-Japan relations since late last year.
  • Recent findings suggest that the encounter, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting, was brief.
  • Observers believe that Takaichi’s brief handshake with Xi reflects a relationship now driven more by security than by trade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi shook hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen last week, the closest thing to a thaw in China-Japan relations since late last year.

Recent findings suggest that the encounter, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting, was brief. Takaichi shook hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, as they greeted arriving guests. Yet apart from a few other brief interactions, Xi and Takaichi held no official meeting.

Observers believe that Takaichi’s brief handshake with Xi reflects a relationship now driven more by security than by trade. Complicating matters is U.S. President Donald Trump’s relationship with Beijing, which Tokyo fears may drive a wedge between Japan and its closest ally.

Relations between Tokyo and Beijing deteriorated sharply in November 2025, when Takaichi told Japan’s parliament that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could prompt Japan to deploy its Self-Defense Forces if the conflict posed an existential threat.

That same month, Beijing demanded that Takaichi retract her comments, calling them “egregious.” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian warned that Japan “must bear all consequences.” He also said that if Japan intervened militarily in a Taiwan Strait conflict, China would “strike back decisively.”.

China advised its citizens to avoid traveling to Japan shortly after Takaichi’s comments in November 2025. It also imposed export restrictions on dual-use technology, including rare earth elements, permanent magnets, and other critical minerals used in defense technologies, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank.

Industry observers note that tensions rose again in March, when a 23-year-old Ground Self-Defense Force officer was arrested after he entered the Chinese embassy in Tokyo while carrying a 7-inch knife. Japan called the incident “regrettable” and noted that the government would take measures to prevent it from taking place again.

In response, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said that the incident had “seriously threatened the safety of embassy personnel and damaged its dignity.”.

In Shenzhen, Takaichi stated Japan’s position on Taiwan had not changed since the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communiqué, which established relations between the two countries.

China considers Taiwan part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force to bring the island under its control.

In a recent development, takaichi received a more subdued welcome than other APEC leaders, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung. Bloomberg reported that Japanese officials asked Beijing to guarantee that Xi would treat Takaichi like other leaders, as a condition of her attendance.

“The Chinese go out of their way to treat the South Koreans and Lee Jae Myung far more warmly than they do Takaichi, a contrast not lost on the Japanese media and government,” Daniel Sneider, a Stanford University professor who specializes in Japan’s foreign policy, says.

China was Japan’s largest trading partner in 2025, with two-way goods trade totaling about $304 billion, according to Japanese government figures.

But with Tokyo and Beijing increasingly viewing each other through a security lens, trade may serve less as a stabilizing force.

“Previously economic relations provided steadying ballast in the overall relationship but now both nations view the relationship more through the security angle and business leaders don’t have the influence they once had,” Jeff Kingston, a Temple University professor who focuses on Japan’s relations with Asia, says.

“Her comments on Taiwan antagonized China and it [Beijing] is not backing down,” he adds.

Sources indicate that still, Japan’s tourism industry has largely held up despite a sharp drop in Chinese arrivals. Local media reported that foreign visitors spent $30.4 billion in the first half of 2026, and October brought in about 3.9 million visitors.

Recent findings suggest that however, visitor numbers from January to October fell 2.5% year on year, to 34.6 million, according to the Asahi Shimbun, citing numbers from the Japan National Tourism Organization. In 2025, Japan welcomed 42.7 million visitors.

Takaichi and Trump met in October 2025, when Trump praised Japan’s first female prime minister and the two countries confirmed trade and rare-earth agreements.

Sources indicate that still, Sneider suggests that, while the U.S. remains a close Japanese ally, Tokyo is closely watching Washington’s engagement with Beijing. “We saw during Xi’s visit to Washington, the Chinese are eager to remind Trump and Americans of the wartime alliance of the U.S. and China against Japan, comments which were strangely echoed by Trump,” he notes.

It has been revealed that when Trump and Takaichi met in March, Trump compared U.S. strikes on Iran with Japan’s 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, which killed more than 2,000 Americans. When asked about why he hadn’t informed allies about his war aims, Trump remarked: “We wanted [a] surprise. Who knows better about surprise than Japan? Why didn’t you tell me about ​Pearl Harbor?”.

Japan views Trump’s meetings with Xi and Russian president Vladimir Putin last week as a “means to isolate Japan and drive wedges between Japan and its ally,” Sneider states.

Takaichi did have one vital bilateral meeting in Shenzhen. On Nov. 18, she met with Putin on the sidelines of the summit. Reuters reported that Takaichi raised two issues with Putin: the detention of a Japanese journalist in Russia and the protection of Japanese companies.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1951 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The 10 deepest S&P 500 declines since 1950 and how long each took to recover

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest stock market corrections since 1950, from the 1957 slide to the 2022 bear market, show how deep S&P 500 declines ran and how long recoveries took.
  • It has been revealed that how far the market falls is only half the story.
  • In early 2020, the S&P 500 lost 33.9% in just 33 days, then hit latest records within five months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest stock market corrections since 1950, from the 1957 slide to the 2022 bear market, show how deep S&P 500 declines ran and how long recoveries took.

It has been revealed that how far the market falls is only half the story. The other half is how long it takes to climb back.

In early 2020, the S&P 500 lost 33.9% in just 33 days, then hit latest records within five months. The dot-com bust was a different animal. The index fell 49.1% from its March 2000 peak and didn't get back to that high until May 30, 2007, more than seven years later.

Both make Plus500's list of the biggest stock market declines since 1950. Over that stretch, Plus500 counts about 38 corrections of 10% or more and 14 bear markets, drops of 20% or more. In other words, corrections are common, and full-blown bear markets are much rarer.

Sources indicate that the 10 declines here run from 1957 to 2022, from the post-war boom and the inflation-wracked 1970s to Black Monday, the financial crisis, the pandemic crash and the 2022 bear market. Their causes repeat: stretched valuations, rising interest rates, inflation, financial stress and the occasional outside shock.

Industry observers note that the list isn't every bear market since 1950. A few near-misses didn't make the cut, including the 19.9% drop tied to the 1990 Gulf War and the 19.3% fall in 1998.

Recent findings suggest that each slide covers the size of the drop, what caused it and how long the index took to recover. Recovery times are measured either from the market's peak or from its bottom, and each slide states which. That choice matters: The same rebound looks a lot shorter counted from the low.

According to recent reports, the S&P 500 fell 56.8% from Oct. 9, 2007, to March 9, 2009, as the housing bust turned into a global financial crisis. Counted from that March 2009 low, the index took about four years to reach its old high, on March 28, 2013.

The rebound started fast: The index rose 68% in the first 12 months after the bottom, according to Plus500. The rest of the climb took much longer.

For some investors, it was the second blow of the decade. Anyone who bought at the March 2000 peak had only just gotten back to even in 2007 when the financial crisis knocked them under water again. They didn't get back above their purchase price for good until 2013, 13 years after buying.

And that's in nominal terms. Getting back to the same dollar amount isn't the same as getting back the same buying power, since inflation had chipped away at those dollars along the way.

According to recent reports, the S&P 500 lost 49.1% from March 24, 2000, to Oct. 9, 2002, falling from 1,527.46 to 776.76. At 929 days, about two and a half years, Plus500 calls it the longest S&P 500 bear market since 1950, measured from peak to bottom.

Sources indicate that the crash grew out of the late-1990s frenzy for tech and internet stocks, many of them valued on the growth investors hoped for rather than profits they actually made. When those hopes faded, tech stocks collapsed. As Plus500 puts it, rate cuts couldn't undo a decade of overvaluation.

The climb back took far longer than the fall. The index didn't regain its March 2000 high until May 30, 2007, more than seven years later. From the 2002 bottom alone, that took about four years and seven months.

The math indicates why. A 49.1% drop isn't erased by a 49.1% gain; that would only get the index back to about 1,158. Returning to 1,527.46 took a gain of about 97%. Put another way, $100 invested at the March 2000 peak was worth about $50.85 at the October 2002 low, before dividends.

The S&P 500 fell 48.2% from Jan. 11, 1973, to Oct. 3, 1974. Getting back to the old high took 90 months from the peak, or 69 months from the bottom. The index didn't return to its 1973 level until July 1980.

The math tells you where the time went: The slide lasted about 21 months. The other five-plus years were spent climbing back.

It happened in the middle of the decade defined by stagflation, stubborn inflation combined with weak growth. Consumer prices more than doubled over the 1970s, according to Plus500, citing Robert Shiller's data.

It has been revealed that that makes even the 90-month figure misleadingly rosy. It tracks only the index's price, not what it could buy. By the time the S&P 500 got back to its 1973 level, those dollars bought far less than they had seven years earlier. In real terms, the wait was longer still.

It has been revealed that the S&P 500 fell 36.1% from Nov. 29, 1968, to May 26, 1970, as the excesses of the 1960s Go-Go bull market ran into inflation, Fed tightening and a recession.

Industry observers note that the Go-Go years had pushed stock prices to stretched levels, leaving the market exposed once the economy turned. Spending on the Vietnam War fueled inflation, the Fed tightened in 1969 and the economy slipped into recession late that year. Stocks turned first, peaking before either the Fed's moves or the downturn.

Sources indicate that then corporate profits shrank. When earnings fall but prices don't, stocks suddenly look even more expensive, and share prices got squeezed.

The decline lasted about 18 months. The index regained its 1968 high on March 6, 1972, 21 months after the bottom and 39 months after the peak. After a 36.1% drop, getting back to even took a gain of about 56.5%.

The S&P 500 lost 33.5% from Aug. 25 to Dec. 4, 1987. The decline is best known for Black Monday, Oct. 19, when the Dow fell 22.6% in a single day, still the largest one-day percentage drop in U.S. stock market history.

The crash came in the middle of the decline, 55 days after the August peak, and the index kept sliding for another 46 days before bottoming.

Plus500 points to four causes: overvaluation, rising interest rates, program trading and portfolio insurance. Program trading used computers to fire off huge batches of orders at once. Portfolio insurance, meant to limit losses, automatically sold stock futures as prices fell, which pushed prices lower and triggered even more selling. There were no circuit breakers to stop the spiral; those didn't exist yet.

Recent findings suggest that the Fed moved promptly. Alan Greenspan, just two months into the job as Fed chair, put out a statement promising to keep money flowing through the financial system, and the Fed cut rates.

In a recent development, unlike most declines on this list, no recession followed. The economy kept growing through 1987 and 1988, and corporate earnings held up. The S&P 500 regained its August high on July 26, 1989, 23 months after the peak and just under 20 months after the bottom.

The S&P 500 fell 33.9% in just 33 days, from a record close on Feb. 19, 2020, to a low on March 23. Plus500 calls it the fastest bear market on record. Most big declines since 1950 took months or years to play out. This one happened in a few weeks.

According to recent reports, the speed came down to the trigger. The selloff was driven by an outside shock, the pandemic, not a breakdown inside the financial system. And the response was enormous.

The Fed cut interest rates to 0%-0.25% on March 15, and on March 23, the day the market bottomed, it announced open-ended bond buying, known as quantitative easing, with no cap on its purchases. Days later, Congress passed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act.

The recovery was just as fast. The index climbed back to its February peak in August 2020, 126 trading days after that high, the fastest bear market recovery in at least 50 years at the time, according to Plus500. Over the 12 months after the bottom, the S&P 500 gained 74%.

All told, 2020 squeezed a full bear market cycle, from record high to bottom and back to a newly introduced record, into about six months.

In a recent development, the S&P 500 fell 27.9% from Dec. 12, 1961, to June 26, 1962, and got back to its old high on Sept. 3, 1963.

Years of post-war optimism had pushed valuations high, especially in hot technology stocks, then nicknamed "tronics.".

The slide is named for President John F. Kennedy, whose administration picked a public fight with the steel industry in April 1962 over price increases. It went well beyond harsh words: The Justice Department opened a grand jury investigation into possible price-fixing, and FBI agents highlighted up at steel companies with subpoenas, according to Time. The clash rattled corporate confidence and hit industrial stocks.

Cold War tensions were rising too, building toward the Cuban Missile Crisis that fall, though the market had already bottomed by then.

Shortly after the low, in July 1962, the Fed cut margin requirements from 70% to 50%, meaning investors could buy stock with less of their own cash. The index took 14 months from the bottom to recover, and 21 months from the peak.

It has been revealed that the S&P 500 fell 25.4% from Jan. 3 to Oct. 12, 2022, as inflation surged and the Federal Reserve raised interest rates aggressively. It then took 15 months from the bottom to reach a latest high, which it finally did on Jan. 19, 2024.

Counted from the January 2022 peak, the full round trip took about two years.

It's the most recent decline on the list, and one of two from the 2020s, along with the COVID crash two years earlier.

In a recent development, for context, Plus500 puts the S&P 500's average gain in the 12 months after a bear market bottom at 47%. That's an average of past recoveries, not a forecast for any single one.

Industry observers note that the S&P 500 fell 27.1% from November 1980 to August 1982. Then it bounced back fast, regaining its prior high in November 1982, just three months after the bottom.

The decline itself ran 622 days, roughly 20 months, much longer than the typical bear market since 1950, which lasted about 13 months on average.

The backdrop was Fed Chair Paul Volcker's war on inflation. To break double-digit price increases, the Fed held interest rates at punishing levels, helping push the economy into a deep recession in 1981 and 1982. Newly elected President Ronald Reagan backed Volcker, giving the Fed the political cover to keep rates high as long as it took.

Counted from the November 1980 peak, the round trip took about two years, almost all of it spent falling. That three-month rebound was far quicker than the 14 months it took after the 1962 Kennedy Slide or the 15 months after the 2022 bear market.

In a recent development, the S&P 500 fell 20.7% from July 15 to Oct. 22, 1957, a quick, 99-day drop that's the only 1950s entry on the list.

Its short length was typical of the era. Declines in the 1950s and 1960s averaged about 178 days, and every one of them recovered within seven to 14 months. The 1957 slide fit that pattern.

It was also the shortest of the three pre-1970 declines on the list, about half as long as the 1962 Kennedy Slide and less than a fifth as long as the 1968-1970 bear market.

Later crashes played out very differently. The dot-com bust and the 1980-1982 bear market each dragged on for well over a year from peak to bottom.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snowflake billionaire Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, are giving more than $22 million to children in their home state of Montana. The couple is putting $1,000 into the Trump Account of every Montana child born in 2023 or 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department announced on Nov. 19.

The gift covers 22,081 children, totaling $22,081,000. The Slootman Family Foundation stated the money has already been deposited through the Treasury Department and invested in the children’s accounts, according to NBC Montana.

It has been revealed that those children were born too early for the federal government’s own $1,000 deposit, which goes only to children born from 2025 through 2028. The Slootmans’ gift gives them the same start. At $1,000 a child, it is also four times the per-child amount in Michael and Susan Dell’s $6.25 billion national pledge.

Industry observers note that “Montana is the Last Best Place,” the Slootmans stated in a statement. “We want to give Montana children an even faster start in life. The money in your account is yours, it cannot be accessed by anybody, not even by you until you are at least 18 years old. What you can do is watch it grow, ask for contributions on birthdays, holidays and other special occasions to make your account compound in value even more.”.

Gov. Greg Gianforte thanked the family for what he called “this significant investment.”.

According to recent reports, frank Slootman, Snowflake’s chairman and former CEO, led the cloud data company through its 2020 initial public offering after taking two other technology companies, Data Domain and ServiceNow, public. Bloomberg Law reported that the Bloomberg Billionaires Index put his net worth at $3.1 billion when the gift was unveiled.

According to recent reports, slootman, born in the Netherlands, has lived in Bozeman for years. When Snowflake eliminated its corporate headquarters in 2021, it named its Bozeman office its principal executive office because Slootman and the tech giant’s CFO lived there, Fortune reported at the time.

It has been revealed that the family foundation has given to Montana causes before, including $1 million to American Prairie Foundation, a conservation group assembling a large prairie reserve in the state, in 2022 and $1.5 million in each of the next two years, according to its tax filings. This gift is on another scale: it roughly matches the $22.7 million in net assets the foundation reported at the end of 2024, the latest year for which its filings are public.

According to recent reports, slootman has also backed Montana Republicans. While he was ServiceNow’s CEO, he gave the maximum allowed contribution to Gianforte, then the state’s congressman, CNBC reported in 2021. Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Montana Republican, publicly thanked the couple for the gift last week, calling it “an incredible bet on Montana’s future.”.

Created under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax law, a Trump Account is a type of individual retirement account for children. Parents, relatives and employers can contribute, generally up to a combined $5,000 a year during childhood. Contributions from charities to a broad group of children, such as every child born in a state in a given year, don’t count toward that cap.

The money goes into low-cost funds that track broad U.S. stock indexes, such as the S&P 500, so its value rises or falls with the market. Investment earnings generally aren’t taxed until you withdraw the money.

According to recent reports, families generally can’t withdraw the money until the calendar year the child turns 18. After that, traditional IRA rules apply, and withdrawals can trigger taxes and early-withdrawal penalties.

According to recent reports, the Treasury Department has opened accounts for eligible children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers. Nearly 70 million children now have one, a White House spokesman told Fortune this month. Only U.S. citizens born from Jan. 1, 2025, through Dec. 31, 2028, qualify for the government’s one-time $1,000 deposit.

According to recent reports, some Montana children covered by the Slootmans’ gift may have already received $250 from Michael and Susan Dell. The Dells’ gift reached 25 million children born from 2016 through 2024, starting in ZIP codes with the lowest median family incomes. The Slootmans’ announcement said 118,523 Montana children are eligible for the Dells’ $250.

A Montana child who qualified for both gifts would have $1,250 from the two couples.

According to recent reports, parents can claim their child’s account through the official Trump Accounts app by verifying their identity and their relationship to the child. Once an account is claimed, relatives can add their own contributions. Fortune has a guide to who gets the $1,000 and how to claim an account.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Recent findings suggest that headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no latest mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Industry observers note that governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain claims nothing moves unless it passes.

It has been revealed that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, debuts alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a newly introduced whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

In a recent development, the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the blueprint, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain indicates it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Sources indicate that scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

Sources indicate that on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain notes it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

Industry observers note that if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement initiative for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

Industry observers note that ethereum is preparing to rebuild some of its most important security foundations. The Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team as developers accelerate a cryptographic overhaul aimed at surviving increasingly capable artificial intelligence and quantum computers.

Ethereum researchers want to change how validators sign messages, how customers authorize transactions, and how Ethereum handles data commitments. The changes reach deep into the machinery protecting the blockchain.

According to recent reports, the Foundation has put the transition on an aggressive timeline, targeting December 2028. Researchers say the work is harder than the Merge, leaving Ethereum with a serious engineering challenge. Ethereum security is becoming a race against technology that keeps improving.

Quantum computers have dominated Ethereum’s long-term cryptographic concerns, and AI is now changing the urgency of that conversation. The Foundation indicates AI models are already finding software vulnerabilities faster than humans can review them. Researchers expect those capabilities to improve, potentially extending into cryptographic research and the mathematical assumptions protecting blockchain networks.

Ethereum isn’t waiting for a machine to crack its cryptography. Developers are preparing for a future where today’s security assumptions could become less reliable, while attackers gain increasingly powerful tools.

The proposed overhaul moves away from elliptic-curve cryptography toward hash-based alternatives. Researchers believe hash-based cryptography offers a more conservative foundation because Ethereum already relies heavily on hash security.

Recent findings suggest that the transition would affect three major areas. Validators would use hash-based keys, wallets would gain a pathway toward hash-based signatures, and data commitments used by rollups would change. This means infrastructure across Ethereum would need to adapt, from staking operators and wallets to multisignature systems.

The challenge is making these changes without breaking the network people already depend on. Bigger signatures could increase hardware demands, while existing tools built around current cryptography would need substantial updates.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026.

According to recent reports, ethereum’s Merge in September 2022 replaced proof-of-work mining with proof-of-stake while keeping the blockchain running. Developers spent years preparing client software, testing networks, and coordinating the transition.

The upcoming overhaul could prove even more difficult. It touches cryptographic components that sit beneath Ethereum’s consensus, account systems, and data infrastructure. Developers have less time, and moving quickly creates more opportunities for mistakes.

That’s why doubling the protocol security team is needed. Formal verification, independent reviews, and extensive testing will need to keep pace with development. A rushed cryptographic migration could create exactly the vulnerabilities Ethereum is trying to eliminate.

The Foundation’s December 2028 target also puts pressure on the wider ecosystem. Wallet developers, staking pools, rollup teams, and node operators will eventually face migration work of their own. The upgrade isn’t something Ethereum’s core developers can finish in isolation.

In a recent development, ethereum’s bet is that preparing early beats waiting for the threat to become obvious. That means potentially delaying other features, rewriting familiar infrastructure, and asking developers to tackle difficult changes before a practical quantum threat arrives.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

In a recent development, stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup confirmed a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

Industry observers note that stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The firm has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

In a recent development, “A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

According to recent reports, sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

According to recent reports, it also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor stated up to 5,000 owners may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

Sources indicate that more than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the tech giant states, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

Industry observers note that stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a organization’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-newly introduced releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity notes its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The manufacturer has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The tech giant indicates it also prepares to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade history spans a century, from a 1924 employee march with zoo animals to giant helium balloons, a wartime pause, wind rules and a pandemic edition.

In 1927, the zoo animals were out and the giant balloons were in. Felix the Cat led the way as the parade's first character balloon, and the idea stuck.

Recent findings suggest that the switch changed what the parade could be. Instead of borrowing animals, Macy's $M could build figures made just for the occasion, and pick characters crowds already knew from movies and comics.

The man behind the balloons was Tony Sarg, a puppeteer and illustrator with a surprisingly global résumé. Born in Guatemala in 1880, he grew up mostly in Germany and worked in London before moving to New York in 1915. In the U.S., he made his name as an illustrator and marionette artist, and his touring manufacturer brought puppet reveals to audiences across the country in the 1920s.

Recent findings suggest that william J. Crawford / Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

Industry observers note that mickey Mouse floated into the parade in 1934, the first Disney $DIS character to get his own balloon. It was only the 11th Macy's $M parade, and the balloon era was still young. Felix the Cat had kicked it off just seven years earlier.

Recent findings suggest that mickey was pretty fresh himself. Walt Disney and animator Ub Iwerks created him in 1928. Their first Mickey short, "Plane Crazy," was a silent film that got a test screening that year but didn't hit theaters until 1929, after a soundtrack was added.

It has been revealed that so Mickey's real debut was "Steamboat Willie," which premiered at New York's Colony Theatre on Nov. 18, 1928. It was one of the first cartoons with synchronized sound, and Walt.

Recent findings suggest that the parade came back on Nov. 22, 1945, after three years off for the war. It was the first one since 1941, and the 19th overall.

By then, the war was over. Germany had surrendered in May, and Japan formally signed its surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on Sept. 2, the date President Harry S. Truman declared V-J Day. That ended nearly four years of American combat. Thanksgiving came less than three months later, while millions of service members were still making their way home.

The timing of the last prewar parade is striking in its own way. It ran on Nov. 20, 1941, just 17 days before the attack on Pearl Harbor, back when the U.S. was still officially neutral.

Recent findings suggest that snoopy joined the parade in 1968, the first character from Charles M. Schulz's "Peanuts" to get a giant balloon.

Recent findings suggest that by then, the strip had been running for 18 years. "Peanuts" debuted in U.S. newspapers on Oct. 2, 1950, and Schulz wrote and drew every strip himself for its entire run.

Snoopy wasn't always the scene-stealer. Early on, he acted a lot like a regular dog. Over time, though, Schulz gave him a rich inner life full of daydreams, a typewriter and a rotating cast of alter egos.

The most famous is the World War I Flying Ace, who perches on top of his red doghouse, imagines it's a Sopwith Camel and takes on the Red Baron.

It has been revealed that "Peanuts" had also made the jump to TV by 1968. "A Charlie Brown Christmas" premiered on CBS in December 1965, followed by "It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown" in October 1966, putting Snoopy in front of a national audience. The Thanksgiving special came later: "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving" didn't air until 1973, five years after the balloon's debut.

Today's parade kicks off at Central Park West and 77th Street on the Upper West Side and ends about 2.5 miles later on 34th Street, right outside Macy's $M Herald Square $SQ.

Industry observers note that the starting line sits next to the American Museum of Natural History, which stretches along Central Park West from 77th to 81st streets. The day before the parade, the balloons are inflated on the side streets around the museum, and that's become an event in its own right. On Wednesday afternoon and evening, crowds stroll past the half-inflated giants pinned down under nets.

On parade morning, the procession heads south down Central Park West, with the park on one side and apartment buildings on the other. At Columbus Circle, it turns east onto Central Park South (the stretch of 59th Street along the bottom of the park), then swings south onto Sixth Avenue.

After the Cat in the Hat accident, New York City set wind limits for the parade balloons. The balloons can't fly if sustained winds top 23 mph or if gusts go above 34 mph.

The rules zero in on the balloons because nothing else in the parade is as exposed. A giant balloon floats several stories above the street, catching every gust, and its handlers can only steer it with lines from the ground. Wind funneling between Manhattan's tall buildings can shove one sideways or push it down without much warning. A float on wheels or a band on foot doesn't have that problem.

The decision came from city government under Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, which made sense: The parade runs on public streets, so flying the balloons became a matter of municipal safety rules, not just.
