No matter how much the parade changes, one thing stays put: Santa Claus comes last. He's closed out every Macy's $M parade since the first one in 1924, trailing every balloon, float, band and performer.

Sources indicate that that makes him one of the parade's few true constants. Balloons have come and gone, the route has shifted and the broadcast has grown from a local program into a national tradition. Through all of it, Santa has held down the final spot.

It's also a reminder of why the parade exists. Macy's created it to sell Christmas, and Santa is the bridge between Thanksgiving morning and the shopping season that kicks off right after. His arrival lands just ahead of Black Friday, traditionally one of the busiest shopping days of the year.

Industry observers note that before it became a Thanksgiving TV staple, the Macy's $M parade was a street party put on by the store's own employees. The first one, in 1924, wasn't even called a Thanksgiving parade. Macy's billed it as the Christmas Parade. Marchers started in Harlem and ended at the flagship store in Herald Square $SQ on 34th Street.

Recent findings suggest that more than a century on, a lot of that still holds. The parade still winds through Manhattan to the same store, and Santa still brings up the rear.

According to recent reports, plenty changed along the way, though, and usually for a reason: a upcoming technology, a wartime shortage, an accident or a pandemic. Live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo were replaced by giant character balloons, which were eventually filled with helium. Then the parade went dark for three years during World War II, when rubber and helium were in short supply.

Industry observers note that it also found an audience far beyond the sidewalk. Footage of the 1946 parade highlights up in "Miracle on 34th Street," released in 1947. TV coverage started with local Upcoming York broadcasts before going national. And the balloons became a running record of American pop culture, from Felix the Cat in 1927 to Mickey Mouse in 1934 and Snoopy in 1968.

Safety rules came later, and the hard way. In 1997, the Cat in the Hat balloon hit a lamppost and seriously injured a spectator, Kathleen Caronna. New York City responded with wind limits, and balloons now stay low or sit out when gusts get too strong. In 2020, the pandemic forced a scaled-down parade with no crowds on the route and most of the action staged around Herald Square.

According to recent reports, the 15 slides ahead trace that history in rough chronological order, with a few on traditions and logistics that span decades. It's not a complete record, just the moments that shaped the parade, and how each one reveals up in this year's 100th edition.

Recent findings suggest that the first Macy's $M parade stepped off on Thanksgiving Day 1924, organized by the store's own employees. It wasn't called a Thanksgiving parade, though. Macy's billed it as the Christmas Parade, and the name noted exactly what it was for. Thanksgiving was the kickoff, and Christmas shopping was the point.

It has been revealed that the route started in Harlem, at 145th Street and Convent Avenue, and ran south through Manhattan to Macy's flagship at Herald Square $SQ. That took marchers from a residential neighborhood all the way to the heart of the city's shopping district.

In a recent development, ending at the store was no accident. Macy's had been on Herald Square, where Broadway crosses Sixth Avenue at 34th Street, since 1902. Finishing at its front door made the connection between the parade and the business hard to miss.

The 1924 parade looked nothing like the one most people picture today. There were no giant balloons. Instead, live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo marched alongside employees in costume, plus floats and bands. The balloons wouldn't arrive for another three years.

In a recent development, santa Claus rode at the very end, as he still does. His arrival closed out the parade and officially opened the store's holiday shopping season.

By then, Macy's was already a major Newly introduced York retailer. Rowland Hussey Macy founded the business in 1858, and a parade on a day when much of the city was off work was a smart way to put the name in front of crowds in person.

That employee-run march was the start of a tradition that would go on to add character balloons, survive a wartime pause and become a TV fixture.

Recent findings suggest that that background made him a natural fit. Sarg's balloons are often described as upside-down marionettes: Instead of strings pulled from above, handlers on the ground steer them with lines from below.

He already had a foot in the door at Macy's, too, designing the store's holiday window displays. The balloons took that window-dressing flair out onto the street.

Recent findings suggest that felix was an easy choice for the debut. The black cat first highlighted up on screen in 1919 and was one of the biggest cartoon stars in the country through the 1920s. Who actually created him is still debated. Producer Pat Sullivan's studio owned the character and put his name on the films, but animator Otto Messmer did much of the drawing.

It has been revealed that either way, the balloon turned a flat, black-and-white cartoon into a three-dimensional star floating over Manhattan. It also set the template the parade still follows: Take a character everyone recognizes and make it enormous.

Sources indicate that in 1928, the parade's balloons got an upgrade: helium. And once the march was over, organizers did something that sounds wild today. They let the balloons go.

Helium made the whole thing work. It's the second-lightest element after hydrogen and much lighter than air, so a helium balloon rises on its own. That's why the parade needs handlers on the ground holding the lines, and why the characters float high above the crowd instead of bobbing along at street level.

According to recent reports, hydrogen could have done the job, too, but it's highly flammable. Helium doesn't burn, which makes it the far safer bet for a giant balloon moving through packed city streets. The danger of hydrogen became painfully clear in 1937, when the hydrogen-filled Hindenburg airship burst into flames while landing in Lakehurst, Latest Jersey.

Sources indicate that releasing the balloons turned the end of the parade into a second show. Instead of deflating them at the finish, crews set them free to drift over the city.

The first attempt didn't go well. The 1928 balloons popped shortly after takeoff. Macy's $M went back to the drawing board and added release valves so the balloons could stay up longer and come down slowly.

According to recent reports, the store also turned it into a game. Each balloon carried a return address, and anyone who found one and mailed it back got a reward.

Recent findings suggest that the stunt didn't last. Macy's eventually stopped the releases, and today crews deflate the balloons after the parade. The helium stayed, though. Nearly a century later, it's still what keeps the lineup in the air.

Recent findings suggest that by the time his balloon made it to Manhattan, Mickey was six years old and already a star. Disney won an honorary Oscar in 1932 for creating him, at the same ceremony where the Disney short "Flowers and Trees" took home the first Academy Award for a cartoon. Mickey had also spread well beyond the movies, with a newspaper comic strip in 1930 and an Ingersoll wristwatch in 1933.

The parade gave him one more stage: the sky over Manhattan, where crowds could watch him drift by overhead.

And Disney was just getting started. Donald Duck made his screen debut in 1934 in "The Wise Little Hen," and "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs," the studio's first full-length animated feature, premiered in 1937.

Mickey's 1934 appearance made him the first Disney character in the Thanksgiving lineup, a decade after Macy's employees marched in the very first parade.

For three Thanksgivings, from 1942 to 1944, there was no Macy's $M parade. World War II had created shortages of the two things the giant balloons couldn't do without: rubber and helium.

Those are the only years the parade has ever been called off since it started in 1924. It even kept going through the worst of the Great Depression.

Rubber was the first problem. After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941, and pulled the U.S. into the war, Japanese forces quickly took over much of Southeast Asia, including Malaya and the Dutch East Indies. That's where most of America's natural rubber came from.

Washington scrambled to hold on to what was left. Tire rationing started in early 1942, and the War Production Board funneled rubber to the military for trucks, planes, jeeps, boots and gas masks. That summer, President Franklin D. Roosevelt asked Americans to turn in their old rubber in a national scrap drive.

According to recent reports, helium was the second problem. At the time, the U.S. produced nearly all of the world's supply, pulled from natural gas fields in the Great Plains. The Navy needed it for blimps that hunted enemy submarines off the coast and escorted convoys.

According to recent reports, with the military claiming both, there was no way to justify a parade. Macy's went a step further than canceling: It deflated its balloons and donated the rubber to the war effort.

The balloons didn't fly over Manhattan again until 1945. Those missing years are also why the parade's numbering lags behind the calendar, and why this year's parade, 102 years after the first one, is the 100th.

In a recent development, the 1945 parade had another first: It was the first one held on a Thanksgiving date set by federal law. In 1939, President Franklin D. Roosevelt had moved the holiday up a week to give stores a longer Christmas shopping season, a push that came straight from retailers. Not every state went along, so for a few years the country had two Thanksgivings, and critics took to calling Roosevelt's version "Franksgiving.".

Congress settled it in December 1941, fixing Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday of November starting in 1942. With no parades from 1942 through 1944, the 1945 march was the first to run under the latest rule, and it's set the date ever since.

In a recent development, that 1945 parade also kicked off a streak that's still going. Macy's $M has held a parade every Thanksgiving since, including the scaled-back 2020 edition during the pandemic.

Recent findings suggest that if you've seen "Miracle on 34th Street," you've seen the 1946 Macy's $M parade. The 20th Century Fox classic, released in 1947, opens with footage of the real thing as it rolled through Manhattan, not a studio re-creation.

That means the crowds on the sidewalks were actual Newly introduced Yorkers watching an actual parade, and the balloons and floats were the ones Macy's built that year. Edmund Gwenn, who played Kris Kringle, even rode in the parade as Santa during the shoot. Anyone who waved at him that morning was unknowingly an extra in a Hollywood movie.

The story starts right there on the route. Kris spots the hired parade Santa drinking and complains, so Doris Walker, the Macy's employee running the parade, asks him to fill in. Maureen O'Hara played Doris. That last-minute swap lands Kris a job as the store's Santa, and the title nods to the flagship's address on West 34th Street.

George Seaton wrote and directed the film, based on a story by Valentine Davies. John Payne played Fred Gailey, a lawyer, and a young Natalie Wood played Doris' daughter, Susan.

It has been revealed that much of the plot plays out in a Latest York courtroom, where a hearing over Kris' sanity turns into a case about whether he really is Santa Claus. The deciding evidence comes from the U.S. Post Office, which delivers a pile of letters addressed to Santa straight to him.

The movie also has fun with Macy's real-life rival, Gimbels. Kris starts sending shoppers to competing stores when Macy's doesn't have what they want, and the goodwill pays off for both.

According to recent reports, it won three Oscars: best supporting actor for Gwenn, best original story for Davies and best screenplay for Seaton. It was also nominated for best picture.

A remake followed in 1994 with Richard Attenborough as Kris, but only the original has the real 1946 parade.

Sources indicate that snoopy even made it to space, sort of. In May 1969, just months after his parade debut, NASA's Apollo 10 crew named their lunar module Snoopy and their command module Charlie Brown.

According to recent reports, macy's $M has flown several Snoopy balloons over the years, including a later one in an astronaut suit. But the 1968 original came first, bringing "Peanuts" into a balloon tradition that started with cartoon characters back in the 1920s.

In a recent development, television is what turned a Manhattan street parade into a national Thanksgiving ritual. Coverage started on local New York stations before going national.

At first, you had to live within range of a New York signal to watch. National broadcasts changed that. Suddenly a family halfway across the country could watch the same balloons drift past the same buildings on Thanksgiving morning.

Recent findings suggest that today, NBC owns the parade on TV. Its live broadcast airs nationwide every Thanksgiving morning, with hosts calling out each balloon, float and performance as it comes into view.

According to recent reports, TV also changed how the parade itself is staged. The stretch in front of Macy's $M Herald Square $SQ flagship doubles as an outdoor set, where performers stop for short numbers before the parade moves on. Casts from current Broadway reveals perform songs from their musicals, the Radio City Rockettes are a fixture and pop stars sing from floats as they pass the cameras. It's the kind of programming a straight procession down the street couldn't deliver on its own.

The balloons are still the stars of the show. Wide shots capture a character at full size against the skyline, while tighter shots show the handlers on the street below, working the lines that keep it on course.

In a recent development, that means viewers at home and fans on the curb experience two different parades. On the sidewalk, you see each unit go by once. On TV, the broadcast cuts between balloons, floats, bands and Herald Square performances, with commentary tying it all together.

For the high school and college marching bands that come from across the country, TV means something else, too: Their friends and families back home can watch them march through Manhattan.

Sixth Avenue, officially the Avenue of the Americas, is the longest leg of the route, carrying the balloons, floats and bands through Midtown toward the finish.

Herald Square gets its name from the Fresh York Herald, a newspaper whose building once stood there. The square itself is the triangle where Broadway crosses Sixth Avenue at 34th Street, and Macy's flagship fills most of the block just to the west, between Broadway and Seventh Avenue.

It has been revealed that the area in front of the store is where the TV performances happen, with Broadway casts, musicians and other acts playing to the cameras. It's reserved for the broadcast and invited guests, so if you're watching in person, you'll want a spot farther up the route.

It has been revealed that streets along the way close to traffic on parade morning, and spectators pack in behind police barricades on both sides. Many show up hours before the first balloon comes into view.

Recent findings suggest that the 1997 parade is remembered for one terrifying moment. On Thanksgiving morning, Nov. 27, strong gusts pushed the Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost. Part of the post broke off and fell into the crowd, seriously injuring Kathleen Caronna, a spectator watching from the sidewalk.

According to recent reports, the balloon was based on the title character of Dr. Seuss' 1957 children's book, with the cat's famous red-and-white striped hat and red bow tie.

According to recent reports, windy weather had made all the balloons hard to handle that day. By 1997, Macy's $M had been flying giant character balloons for 70 years, and the system hadn't changed much: Each one is steered by a team of handlers on foot, holding ropes and adjusting the balloon's height and direction as they walk.

That works fine in calm air. But a giant balloon catches wind like a sail, and a sudden gust can shove it sideways or drag it down faster than anyone on the ground can react. Handlers can pull their lines in, but a strong enough gust will still push a balloon off course.

Manhattan makes that especially dangerous. The route is lined with streetlights, traffic signals and trees, and spectators stand just a few feet from where the balloons pass overhead. A balloon blown off its path doesn't have anywhere safe to go.

The accident pushed New York City officials to rethink when the balloons should be allowed to fly at all.

On parade morning, the NYPD and Macy's keep a close eye on conditions. There are weather monitoring stations along the route, and each giant balloon's assistant pilot carries a wind meter that an NYPD representative also tracks. The final call on the balloons comes just before the parade starts, based on real-time data from along the route.

Grounding isn't the only option. When gusts pick up, handlers can fly a balloon lower to keep it in the parade rather than pulling it entirely. Macy's trains its volunteer handlers ahead of time for exactly that.

The limits apply only to the balloons. Floats, bands, performers and Santa's sleigh roll on regardless.

For spectators, that means the balloon lineup is never quite set in stone. Whether your favorite character shows up depends on the forecast as much as on Macy's intends.

In a recent development, in 2020, the parade went on, but without the crowds. With COVID-19 still raging, Macy's $M shrank the event down to the blocks around its Herald Square $SQ flagship and turned it into a made-for-TV show.

According to recent reports, the 94th parade took place on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 26, 2020, while New York City was still limiting large gatherings. Macy's opted for a smaller parade instead of canceling, and that decision kept 2020 in the official count. Without it, this year's parade wouldn't be the 100th.

It has been revealed that herald Square was a natural choice. It's already where the TV performances happen every year, so for viewers, the 2020 parade still looked like the one they knew.

The biggest change was how the balloons flew. Normally, teams of handlers walk alongside each balloon, steering it with guide lines. In 2020, Macy's tethered the balloons to anchor vehicles instead, which meant far fewer people crowded together in the street.

Industry observers note that everything else was scaled back, too. Participants wore masks and kept their distance, and the high school and college marching bands chosen for 2020 stayed home. Macy's invited them back for the following year instead.

In 2021, the crowds returned, the parade went back to its full route and the handlers were back on their feet.

Santa doesn't walk the route. He rides a sleigh float past the crowds and all the way to the finish outside Macy's Herald Square $SQ.

Recent findings suggest that on TV, the whole broadcast builds toward him, and his arrival is the substantial finale. Macy's bills it as the official start of the holiday season.

Sources indicate that the connection doesn't stop at the parade, either. Macy's Herald Square is also home to Santaland, where kids can visit Santa throughout the holidays, so the guy who closes the parade is waiting for them at the same address.

Santa has made it through every major interruption, from the wartime pause to upcoming safety rules to the pandemic. However the parade changes, he's still the last one down the street.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning—or should I say, good grief? Jensen Huang’s 11-day timeout ended yesterday as Nvidia’s board unanimously reinstated him as CEO, having last week rejected his offer to return. Investors cheered, sending the stock up 30% on the news, although S&P 500 futures already pointed to a rebound in the market. His colleagues cheered, perhaps for fiscal rather than emotional reasons amid allegations that their old boss often belittled them and slept with a direct report. Elon Musk declared that “the mistake has been corrected” while fellow X influencer Bill Ackman wrote that “the wisdom of the crowd prevails.” And President Donald Trump took credit for the move, with a spokesman telling Fortune “we have to protect our geniuses.”.

If you felt a pit in your stomach at hearing the news, you’re not alone. Even the prediction markets didn’t spot this one coming as Huang faces a plethora of probes, investigations, lawsuits, and questions over whether he compromised national security, misled investors, violated corporate policies, and more. When the scandal first broke, several leaders told me Huang had to go, even though it might trigger a selloff. Nvidia remains a cautionary tale on the perils of an unchecked CEO and an ecosystem that relies too much on one player to sustain everyone else’s success. But that concentration of power and the intensity of the global AI race also created a compelling case to bring Huang back.

In a recent development, I reached 14 Fortune 500 and Global 500 manufacturer leaders yesterday, four of whom are women, to get their anonymous take. A few themes emerged:.

Recent findings suggest that A bad look for brand America. One leader called it “an embarrassment for our country to see how far we’ve dropped as a role model in leadership.” Another CEO argued that Trump’s involvement gave Americans more proof of the crony capitalism they just voted against, giving a fresh Congress more reason to investigate and regulate. Several suggested checking to see if any officials traded Nvidia stock in advance of the news, given the president’s penchant for making money on the job. One non-U.S. CEO was especially disappointed that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent extended an olive branch after initially taking a tough stance against Nvidia, arguing it suggests that “even U.S. security and rule of law can now take a back seat to profit.”.

A mixed look for brand AI. In an industry that’s struggling to show Americans the “good” in AI, one leader noted, this is yet another step in the opposite direction. Another take from a prominent CEO: “Now there’s proof of systemic risk because the power is concentrated in such a small group of people who rely on each other’s capital and technology for success.” A leader in the AI space acknowledged “a cult of personality” around Huang but remarked the investor panic over his exit reinforces how critical he is to Nvidia and America’s AI race against China: “You have to sometimes make shitty decisions, but without him, we’re in a bad place,” they said. “It’s not worth the risk.”.

A bad look for Nvidia. Leaders were especially critical of the board for failing to have a succession strategy and for reversing its stance amid mounting investigations. Several were blunt when I asked if Huang should have been reinstated: “No. The guy (allegedly) slept with a direct report. End of story.” Another pushed back when I used the term “prodigal” to describe Huang, saying “that would imply he’s repentant.” And one CEO pondered the message this gives to Huang’s colleagues, including the women who dared to speak up about his alleged affairs. It will also be harder to fire future leaders who have inappropriate relationships and anyone who was fired in the past now has grounds to sue.

Recent findings suggest that the apparent lack of consequences for Huang bothered several leaders, with one calling it a “troubling precedent,” noting that “when an executive is deemed indispensable, accountability becomes negotiable.” As one CEO put it: “I liked Lloyd Blankfein’s mentioning of de Gaulle’s quote that ‘the graveyards are filled with indispensable men.’” All signals point to a return to the status quo, with Huang going back to his “founder mode” of having 60 direct reports. Interim CEO Colette Kress can go back to being CFO, where she’s facing an SEC investigation into accounting practices. But some things do change. An Nvidia customer told me yesterday that the business relationship will continue but “there’s never going to be the same trust.”Contact CEO Daily via Diane Brady at diane.brady@fortune.com.

Gwynne Shotwell made Musk’s rocket business work. Can she do the same for AI in space?

Industry observers note that spaceX president Gwynne Shotwell has spent two decades winning customers and turning Elon Musk’s ideas into businesses. Now she has to make his blueprint for AI data centers in orbit pay off—even as experts interviewed by Fortune question whether they can compete on cost with those on Earth.

The COO behind Kalshi’s meteoric climb.

Industry observers note that luana Lopes Lara went from Bolshoi-trained ballerina to MIT math prodigy to, at 30, the world's youngest female self-made billionaire. As Kalshi's COO, she runs most of the $40 billion prediction market that overtook Polymarket, and she once bet the firm on suing regulators. Now she faces her toughest fight: states arguing Kalshi's sports trading is gambling.

Meta’s AI chief warns humans could lose control of self-improving AI.

Alexandr Wang warns that people could lose control of AI once it learns to improve itself. He pointed to a claimed AI-assisted solution to the Riemann hypothesis, a famously unsolved math problem. Mathematicians have yet to verify the claim.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • While the market is still struggling with volatility and rapidly declining investor interest, the latest on-chain data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows that futures traders have become extremely active on Binance.
  • The data reveals that both Bitcoin and Ethereum have seen their perpetual futures trading volume on Binance surge to a combined high of $39.8 billion as of November 20.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by volume, Binance is witnessing a rapid surge in its futures trading activity as the broader crypto market continues to face increased selling pressure.

While the market is still struggling with volatility and rapidly declining investor interest, the latest on-chain data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows that futures traders have become extremely active on Binance.

The data reveals that both Bitcoin and Ethereum have seen their perpetual futures trading volume on Binance surge to a combined high of $39.8 billion as of November 20.

Notably, this marks the highest level the metric has reached since September 21, indicating that traders are actively adjusting their positions to hedge against further losses as volatility continues to intensify.

Nonetheless, Bitcoin saw the highest increase in perpetual futures volume as it surged to $24.75 billion on the same day.

The data further showed that the volume was slightly higher than the $24.57 billion recorded on September 21, when Bitcoin was trading above $87,000.

Ethereum, on the other hand, followed with a notable increase in the same metric, recording $15.05 billion in perpetual futures volume on the same day.

However, Ethereum did not entirely mimic Bitcoin in the trend as this was still below the $17.27 billion recorded during the September 21 trading period.

Further data shows that the high futures trading activity recorded on Binance on November 20 has coincided with BlackRock’s record Bitcoin ETF outflow.

The data shows that BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $511 million in net outflows on that day, marking a sharp reversal from the positive inflows seen in September.

While this shows that investors are also pulling their funds from Bitcoin ETFs, it marked the highest single-day outflow BlackRock has ever recorded.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern.
  • By 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

That pattern is about to break.

By 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

Two major datasets show how far the dashboard has drifted from reality:.

It has been revealed that on a typical board dashboard, the throughput gains appear as headline numbers while the instability sits in a footnote. A director reading deployment frequency would see an organization getting faster, with no view of the review process thinning out underneath it.

DORA has acknowledged the gap. Its researchers introduced deployment rework rate, the proportion of deployments that are unplanned fixes, as a fifth measure in 2024. DORA’s Nathen Harvey said on DX’s Engineering Enablement podcast that the four keys aren’t sufficient on their own for understanding AI’s impact.

Rework rate is worth tracking, but it records the fix only after a customer has already hit the bug. It can’t warn you before a release.

It has been revealed that code coverage reports how much of a codebase some test executed. It claims nothing about whether that test checked an outcome a customer cares about, and AI-generated test suites can push coverage up without improving that second question.

A suite can touch every branch of a checkout service and still never confirm that a customer paying in a second currency gets charged the right amount.

You build verification coverage from the customer side. Product, engineering and finance agree on the journeys that make or lose money: signup, checkout, the core action the product exists for and the permission flows enterprise buyers probe during procurement.

Each journey gets an expected outcome written in business terms, such as an order confirmed at the correct price or an invited user landing with the right role. For each release, the team records how many of those journeys it ran end to end on the release candidate, in real browsers and devices, and how many produced that outcome.

A CFO can read the result without a glossary: something like “47 of 52 revenue-critical journeys verified before release.” Because your team measures it before anything ships, it should move ahead of rework rate and change failure rate, which register problems only after customers find them.

Part of the pressure comes from outside engineering. Cyber underwriters have started asking CFOs how they are managing AI risk.

Directors who signed off on AI tooling budgets will also start asking what the spend bought besides volume. A rising deployment count tells them the team ships more often. Verification coverage tells them whether the product customers pay for still works.

Most teams can produce a first figure within a quarter by following four steps:.

Agentic test automation platforms such as KaneAI now let teams run these journeys against the rendered product on every release candidate.

DORA metrics still belong on the dashboard, because they tell you how fast and how steadily your organization delivers. Add verification coverage beside them in your next monthly report, and protect it from the pressure every board metric attracts.

A team under pressure can raise its score by shortening the journey list. Require product and finance sign-off before anyone changes it, and show the list size next to the ratio.

Include the failure cases customers hit, such as a declined card or an expired session, because a journey verified only on its happy path tells the board less than the number suggests.

Sources indicate that expect the score to sit below 100%, and tell directors which journeys failed and why. When they ask what AI has changed, you can show them how much of what shipped was verified to work.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

That pattern is about to break.

Recent findings suggest that by 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

#167673. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • According to recent reports, now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

According to recent reports, now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

Recent findings suggest that no. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful fresh AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

It has been revealed that the question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the tech giant has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remarked Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

It has been revealed that some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

According to recent reports, MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Strategy) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

Sources indicate that MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

In a recent development, full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

In a recent development, over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

It has been revealed that what happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the tech giant with reports.

According to recent reports, the first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

According to recent reports, moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Sources indicate that since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

Industry observers note that in theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Sources indicate that microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple owners to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

Recent findings suggest that more broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

Industry observers note that the cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to matter OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are vital enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he noted, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

According to recent reports, think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Sources indicate that here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Recent findings suggest that managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

Industry observers note that it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

Industry observers note that it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

Afterward, her friend suggested Shotwell stop by his upcoming company to meet the owner.

The owner, of course, was Elon Musk. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and claims it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

Sources indicate that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It notes TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

Recent findings suggest that the card is also more candid than most. It indicates TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

In a recent development, here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Industry observers note that read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

According to recent reports, the AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card reveals the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a substantial generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 latest tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card states all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

Industry observers note that the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

It has been revealed that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

5 Powerful Lessons Leaders Can Learn From People Who Pay It Forward

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • When my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard.
  • Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

I founded the William S.D. Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind. Over the next three decades, I watched scholars build careers, support families and, in many cases, create opportunities for others. This year, the Foundation sought to understand those outcomes more systematically. It surveyed and interviewed former scholars, publishing its findings in a white paper, Opening Doors Through Education. The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

The findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. Former scholars described how their education helped them build careers, improve their families’ circumstances and contribute to their communities. Many have also gone on to support others through mentoring, volunteering and philanthropy, extending the benefits of their education to people they may never have reached otherwise.

According to recent reports, while the research is exploratory and cannot establish cause and effect, it raises questions that extend well beyond philanthropy. Every organization invests in people, yet few measure what those investments make possible over a lifetime. Here are five lessons I believe leaders can take from our experience.

The paper introduces a measure called the William Louey Effect: the difference between the path a scholar actually followed and the one that might reasonably have been expected given their starting circumstances. The name matters less than the question behind it: compared with what?

Sources indicate that businesses regularly celebrate employees who complete leadership programs and subsequently earn promotions. But would those employees have succeeded without the training? A talented person who was already destined to thrive tells us relatively little about the program. Someone whose trajectory genuinely changed tells us considerably more.

Leaders should examine starting circumstances, not simply final achievements. Otherwise, they risk rewarding programs for identifying talent rather than developing it.

One of our paper’s most striking findings is also among its most uncertain. It estimates that parental income is approximately 46% less predictive of our scholars’ adult earnings than it is nationally in China, comparing coefficients of 0.27 and 0.50. But that estimate draws on income ranges reported by roughly 10 people, all originally selected for academic promise. Some of the difference might have existed without our support.

The same problem affects corporate high-potential programs. When participants outperform their peers, how much credit belongs to the program, and how much to the selection process? Good measurement requires intellectual humility. Leaders should distinguish between outcomes they observe and impact they can reasonably attribute to their intervention. Acknowledging uncertainty does not weaken a success story. It makes the conclusions more credible.

It has been revealed that from the beginning, I encouraged scholars to pay their opportunities forward when they felt ready, whether through money, knowledge or time. I never wanted that expectation to become a condition of receiving support. The paper calls this voluntary reciprocity: giving that emerges from gratitude and personal conviction rather than contractual obligation.

Organizations often seek loyalty through retention bonuses, repayment clauses and restrictive agreements. Such mechanisms can serve legitimate purposes, but they cannot manufacture genuine commitment. Some of our earliest scholars independently established and funded a scholarship for Chinese students at Oxford. We did not require them to do so, because when people feel trusted rather than indebted, they have the freedom to turn an opportunity they received into something of their own.

Recent findings suggest that generosity becomes more powerful when people can see what it looks like. Several scholars who established the Oxford scholarship also mentor its recipients, offering guidance similar to the support they once received. They are passing forward not only financial resources, but a way of treating people.

The leadership lesson is practical. If you want employees to mentor colleagues, share knowledge and create opportunities, make those expectations visible through your own behavior. Take time to advise younger employees, introduce promising people to contacts who can help them, and continue supporting colleagues even when there is no immediate benefit to you. Then give others the freedom to contribute in their own ways.

Recent findings suggest that A culture of generosity cannot be built through instructions alone. It grows when people repeatedly experience the behavior their leaders advocate.

We have never asked a scholar to repay their scholarship. Instead, many have supported relatives, mentored students or helped others pursue opportunities. One former scholar described the experience as bringing philanthropy forward by a generation. For business leaders, this suggests a broader definition of return on investment.

Consider an employee who leaves your company and becomes an exceptional manager elsewhere, or a former trainee who mentors people you will never meet. Your organization may receive no direct financial benefit, yet its investment continues producing value. Traditional performance dashboards rarely capture that contribution.

Recent findings suggest that our paper argues that measuring educational outcomes only at graduation or the first job can overlook changes that emerge much later, including leadership, entrepreneurship and upward mobility. The same applies to professional development. A program evaluated after 12 months may reveal little about the influence its participants eventually have on others. Leaders should consider staying connected with former employees and tracking how their contributions evolve, without treating their subsequent achievements as corporate property.

The Foundation offers its framework as a starting point, not a definitive answer. We hope other scholarship providers and universities will test it with larger groups and more rigorous comparisons. Business leaders need not adopt our terminology to apply the underlying principle.

According to recent reports, when deciding whether an investment in people has succeeded, ask two questions: What did this person achieve, and what did they subsequently make possible for others? The second is harder to measure, and its benefits may never return directly to the organization that made the investment. But three decades after founding the Foundation, I have come to believe it may be the more notable question.

In a recent development, when my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

Recent findings suggest that the findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

A newly introduced baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

It has been revealed that “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla noted. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

According to recent reports, birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has problems with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Industry observers note that gangiredla stated the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

Sources indicate that if you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

According to recent reports, the platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for people.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on fresh parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

Industry observers note that how universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — major metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your manufacturer?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

It has been revealed that earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our manufacturer has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin reportedly became available at a massive discount on Kraken after a sharp dislocation in Kraken's dollar trading markets.

Users reported being able to purchase BTC for as little as 24,250 CAD, equivalent to $16,900 at that time.

Apparently, the incident has only affected the BTC/CAD trading pair on the platform, although some consumers claim the disruption appeared across several CAD markets.

The cause the glitch is still unclear, while the reported transactions are yet to be verified.

The incident might have involved thin liquidity problem in Kraken's CAD order books.

Large sell orders reportedly overwhelmed available buy orders, leaving insufficient demand to absorb the selling pressure.

According to some accounts, at one point about 20 BTC was being sold every 15 minutes, causing the imbalance to push BTC price against CAD further down.

One such transaction resulted in BTC price at around C$24,250, or $16,900. Compared with Bitcoin trading between $57,000-$58,000, the discount amounted to a staggering 71%. Other users reported BTC briefly trading around $27,000.

In a recent development, kraken's status page continued to show its systems as operational during the incident. No official explanation from the exchange was available at the time of writing.

Industry observers note that the reported dislocation highlights the risks associated with trading in markets with limited liquidity. When an order book lacks sufficient buy-side depth, even relatively large sell orders can cause prices to move sharply away from the broader market.

Recent findings suggest that on Friday, Bitcoin price dropped below $60,000. At some point, it fell 5.10% to $55,830, the lowest level since September 2024.

Recent findings suggest that liquidations on crypto exchanges reached $1.57 billion over 24 hours on Nov. 20.

According to CoinGlass, 265,525 traders were liquidated over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of the total.

According to recent reports, bitcoin saw $554.28 million in liquidations, and 91.3% of that amount came from long positions. Ethereum (ETH) fell below $1,700 on Nov. 20, and ETH traders saw $331.08 million in liquidations.

Binance accounted for 45.8% of all liquidations, and the largest single order was also on Binance: an $11.98 million ETH/USDT long position that was liquidated at $1,638.78.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano is facing fresh criticism for struggling to attract owners and generate on-chain activity, despite being nearly nine years into its development.

Widely-followed crypto analyst Lark Davis has branded the network a “largely failed blockchain,” pointing to a stark adoption gap with Solana, which launched four years later but has significantly outpaced ADA in daily users, perpetual futures trading volume, and application revenue.

Despite having nearly a decade to establish itself in the blockchain industry, Cardano continues to face questions about its ability to attract people and generate meaningful network activity. Analyst Lark Davis has commented on the adoption gap between Cardano and Solana, arguing that Solana has significantly outperformed ADA despite launching four years later.

“Nine years in and Cardano is still waiting on adoption,” Davis wrote on X.

According to Davis, Cardano accounts for just around 1% of Solana’s daily people, highlighting the stark difference in activity between the two networks. The gap reportedly extends beyond user numbers, with Cardano recording only about 0.3% of Solana’s perpetual futures trading volume.

In a recent development, the revenue figures paint an even more challenging picture for the Cardano ecosystem. Davis estimates that Cardano generates roughly 0.2% of the application revenue recorded across Solana’s ecosystem, further highlighting the difference in economic activity between the competing networks.

Based on these figures, Davis delivered a particularly harsh assessment of Cardano, describing it as a “largely failed blockchain.” His criticism centers on the contrast between Cardano’s nine-year journey and Solana’s ability to build a considerably larger user base and generate more trading activity and application revenue in a shorter period.

It has been revealed that the latest criticism follows a series of similar remarks from Davis about Cardano’s adoption challenges. As ZyCrypto previously reported, the analyst had also taken aim at Cardano over its relatively small user base, questioning the network’s ability to attract and retain customers despite years of development.

Despite his harsh assessment of Cardano’s fundamentals, Davis has occasionally expressed optimism about ADA’s price prospects.

In November 2025, for instance, he suggested that Cardano could stage a rally similar to XRP’s 2024 surge, pointing to the strength of its community and brand as potential catalysts.

More recently, on September 28, Davis argued that Cardano’s “cult following” could help drive ADA back toward $1, with further upside potentially taking the token to $1.50 or even $2.

However, these bullish price projections focused more on speculative market demand and Cardano’s dedicated community than on measurable improvements in network adoption or ecosystem activity.
